lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P091949, loan IBRD-75420 of US$38.40 million for the Gansu Cultural and Natural Heritage Protection and Development Project, approved 20 March 2008, effective 11 August 2008, closed 30 June 2015 after two restructurings; US$35.02 million was disbursed. companies.name: Gansu Provincial Development and Reform Commission
companies.role: Implementing agency. The completion report names it as the implementing agency and places the Provincial Project Management Office inside it. No contractor is named in the documents.

cases.community: Nine sites were funded. Two of them took land and houses: the Lutusi Ancient Government Center tourism area at Liancheng and the Qingcheng Ancient Town heritage area. The Bank's completion report gives the finished figures for both together: 14 households relocated, 19.54 mu of land permanently acquired and 870.71 square metres of housing pulled down, with 26 households and 123 people affected either permanently or temporarily. All of the relocation and all of the demolition happened at Lutusi; its table shows 17 households planned against 14 actual, and 1,241.49 square metres of housing planned against 870.71 actual. The report rates the resettlement work moderately satisfactory for two reasons it names: water and electricity were slow to reach the resettlement houses at Lutusi, and the site chosen for seven households was not accepted by all of them. The refusal ended the plan for the site's car park, and the land acquisition for it was dropped. The report also says no complaint was received during the project and that compensation for land and houses was at least as high as the resettlement plans set out.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2015. The completion report says land acquisition and resettlement cost more than twice the estimate, which it attributes to compensation rates and costs rising over the life of the project. The report's body text gives the estimate as RMB 2.76 million and the final cost as RMB 5.80 million; the actual column of its own Table A6-1 gives RMB 5.79 million, and the report does not explain the difference. It does not say when water and electricity reached the Lutusi resettlement houses. The report also gives two different planned household figures: its body text says the appraisal estimated 34 households, while the planned column of Table A6-1 gives 17. It does not reconcile them.

Five safeguard policies were triggered: involuntary resettlement OP 4.12, environmental assessment OP 4.01, natural habitats OP 4.04, physical cultural resources OP 4.11 and safety of dams OP 4.37. The Bank's completion report of 18 December 2014 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, borrower performance Satisfactory, and risk to the development outcome Low or Negligible; it rates the carrying out of the resettlement plan Moderately Satisfactory because land acquisition difficulties held up the works. cases.community: The complex is a dam, a ship lock and a hydropower station on the middle Gan River, with flood protection works. The Bank's completion report says that when it was finished the project had permanently acquired 654.9 hectares of land, against an appraisal estimate of 615 hectares, and temporarily acquired 70.6 hectares against an estimate of 330 hectares, and that 141 households comprising 515 people were relocated, against an appraisal estimate of 169 households comprising 597 people. The appraisal document says the works would affect about 53 villages and one state farm in Taihe County. The report records that some activities fell behind schedule, naming the building of the Huangkeng resettlement site and the land acquisition for the Dongmen canal in the Wanhe protection area, and that land acquisition for the Donggang diversion canal ran into difficulties that forced the engineering design to be changed. It also says special financial and physical help was given to the vulnerable households identified, that some farmland was raised to cut flooding, and that an outside agency monitored the resettlement every six months and confirmed that it met the Bank's requirements.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2014 and the ship lock was built. The completion report says the lock's full capacity will only be used by about 2020, because the Xiajiang lock downstream was finished in May 2014. The completion report's cost table carries land acquisition and resettlement on two lines, both in US dollars and both in the counterpart column with no Bank loan amount against them: US$2.13 million planned and US$2.17 million actual for the complex itself, and US$28.65 million planned and US$28.87 million actual for the flood protection works.

cases.title: A Uyghur herders' village flooded and demolished for the Ertanggou reservoir
cases.place: Tuyamar village, Qialekan administrative village, Shanshan County, Turpan, Xinjiang, China
cases.point: The Ertanggou dam. The resettlement plan gives the dam's position as 89 degrees 53 minutes east and 43 degrees 18 minutes north, converted here to decimal degrees.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P111163, loan IBRD-79340 of US$100 million for the Xinjiang Turfan Water Conservation Project, approved 17 June 2010, effective 28 October 2010, closed 31 March 2017; the full US$100 million was disbursed. Environmental category A. Seven safeguard policies were triggered: environmental assessment OP 4.01, natural habitats OP 4.04, pest management OP 4.09, physical cultural resources OP 4.11, indigenous peoples OP 4.10, involuntary resettlement OP 4.12 and safety of dams OP 4.37. The Bank's completion report of 13 October 2017 rates the outcome Highly Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory, borrower performance Satisfactory, and risk to the development outcome Moderate. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 22 November 2017 agrees on the first four ratings and prints the risk rating as Modest.

companies.name: Turpan Prefecture Water Resources Bureau
companies.role: Implementing agency, the prefectural water authority in Xinjiang; its project management office ran the works. The resettlement itself was carried out by the Shanshan County government, which set up a project leading group and a resettlement office for it. No construction contractor is named in the documents.

cases.community: The project built three reservoirs to store water upstream: Alagou, Meiyaogou and Ertanggou. The Ertanggou reservoir flooded a hamlet called Tuyamar village, known as the Ertanggou villager group of Qialekan administrative village. The Bank's completion report says the reservoir affected 103 people in 26 households, all of them Uyghur herders, and that the whole village was inundated and the houses demolished. The report prints an inundation inventory of 4,774.36 square metres of houses, 14.11 mu of arable land, 21.37 mu of orchard, 35.05 mu of man-made pasture, 700 mu of natural pasture, 167.86 mu of forestry land, 2.5 kilometres of pasture road and one hydrological station. Every figure in that table also stands, to the decimal, in the reservoir’s 2009 resettlement plan, where the housing line reads "the area of houses which will be resettled is 4774.36 m2". The report gives the table as impact and the plan gives it as forecast, and no document says the two were measured again at the end. Four more households who lived outside the village but owned assets in it are counted inside the 103. Nobody living around the Alagou and Meiyaogou reservoirs was affected, and a few trees and other assets lost there were compensated. Shanshan County built a new site 15 kilometres away in a Uyghur neighbourhood, with 29 house yards of 1,300 square metres each, water and power, a road, a small clinic, a grocery store, a new mosque and an enlarged primary school in the next village. Each household was given a set of furniture worth RMB 5,000. For the resettlers' livelihoods, 14 hectares of desert land was reclaimed at the new site and 818 metres of irrigation canals were built; the report says the soil was highly saline at first and the households were given technical help with it. The report says their living standards were restored and improved and that they were satisfied with the compensation. A survey of 10 of the 26 households by the project's outside monitor puts average household income at RMB 41,646 in 2014 against RMB 28,175 before the move.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 31 March 2017. The completion report's cost table gives the resettlement as budgeted at 22,156.8 thousand yuan and spent at 20,229.7 thousand yuan, with the rural resettlement line itself spending more than planned and other lines less. Shanshan County added Y27.63 million of its own for housing and productive infrastructure at the new site, which the report says brought the total to Y47.86 million, double the original budget. The report says the herders had stopped pasturing with a subsidy of RMB 3,500 a person a year, and attributes that pause to a hill-closure campaign for ecological rehabilitation run by Turpan Prefecture rather than to the project. A new pasture road was built along the mountains at the herders' request.

cases.displaced_label: 26 households relocated, 103 people affected (World Bank completion report, 2017)
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 108 for this project. The Bank's completion report counts 103 people in 26 households at Tuyamar village, says the whole village was inundated and the houses demolished, and describes their relocation to a new site 15 kilometres away. The figure 103 also appears in the project's 2009 resettlement plan, which projected "resettlers in the planning year of the project construction will reach 103 in 21 households"; the household count differs between the two documents, 21 planned against 26 in the completion report, which also records 29 house yards built.
cases.ecosystem: The reservoir flooded 700 mu of natural pasture, 35.05 mu of man-made pasture and 167.86 mu of forestry land. Those three figures are in the completion report's inundation table and also, unchanged, in the 2009 resettlement plan that forecast them. The new site was made by reclaiming 14 hectares of desert land, which the report says was highly saline at first.
cases.confidence_note: The World Bank's own completion report and the Evaluation Group's review of that report are the only sources found. The lender is reporting on its own project and rates the outcome Highly Satisfactory. No independent press report, court record or field study of this village's move was found; a Chinese-language search on the reservoir and county names returned nothing about it. The report's account of the destination is favourable throughout and rests on the project's own external monitor, whose income survey covers 10 of the 26 households. The completion report's whole inundation inventory, including the 4,774.36 square metres of housing and the 103-person count, is the 2009 resettlement plan's forecast table reprinted without change, so none of those figures is an independent measurement of what was lost. What the completion report states in its own words, and the plan does not, is that the village was inundated, the houses were demolished, 26 households were resettled to a site 15 kilometres away and 29 house yards were built; the plan had forecast 20 households, rising to 21. The completion report also places Tuyamar village in Jinsheng township of Turpan city in one paragraph while the same document has Shanshan County carrying out the resettlement; it does not explain the difference. The two documents give the risk rating under different words: the report says Moderate and the review's column says Modest.

cases.title: Site engineer killed on the Lubuk Alung to Kuraitaji road works
cases.place: Lubuk Alung to Kuraitaji road, Padang Pariaman, West Sumatra, Indonesia
cases.point: Lubuk Alung, the northern end of the 16.23-kilometre road section the completion report names as package 21A. Village centre from OpenStreetMap; the report gives no coordinates for the spot where the engineer was hit.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P090990, loan IBRD-80430 for the Western Indonesia National Roads Improvement Project, approved 26 May 2011, effective 12 March 2012, closed 30 June 2021 after four restructurings. The Bank's completion report of 14 December 2021 gives the loan as US$250 million originally, revised to US$228 million, with US$224,160,404 disbursed; its cover page states the amount as SDR 145.63 million. Environmental category B, partial assessment. Three safeguard policies were triggered, per the appraisal document's own table: environmental assessment OP 4.01, physical cultural resources OP 4.11 and involuntary resettlement OP 4.12. The same table marks natural habitats OP 4.04, forests OP 4.36, indigenous peoples OP 4.10 and safety of dams OP 4.37 as not triggered. The report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and the quality of monitoring and evaluation Substantial. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 7 June 2022 agrees on outcome and Bank performance but rates monitoring and evaluation Modest, giving shortcomings in its design as the reason. The two documents give different totals for what the project cost: the completion report's financing table gives US$224,160,404 both as the amount disbursed under the loan and as the total project cost, while the Evaluation Group's review prints US$223,780,891.76 as the total project cost and US$224,160,404.03 as the actual amount. Neither document explains the difference.

companies.name: Directorate General of Highways, Ministry of Public Works and Housing, Indonesia
companies.role: Implementing agency. The Directorate General of Highways is the national roads authority inside Indonesia's public works ministry; it ran the works through a project management unit and project implementation units in the provinces. The completion report does not name the supervision firm or the civil works contractor for package 21A.

cases.community: The loan paid for widening and rehabilitating national road sections along the western Sumatra corridor, and later for road repairs in Central Sulawesi. The Bank's completion report records that a fatal traffic accident happened on road package 21A on 27 July 2019, in which a site engineer working for the project's design and supervision consultants was killed. The report gives the cause as human error, a car travelling at about 60 kilometres an hour hitting him from behind while he was taking photographs in the middle of the carriageway, and says the accident "could have been prevented if adequate traffic management provisions would had been deployed". Package 21A was the 16.23-kilometre Lubuk Alung to Kuraitaji section, a second contract procured to finish works left by package 21 on the same section, which the report says was terminated in June 2019 for the contractor's poor performance. The report's table of road packages gives 21A a commencement date of 3 January 2019 and a taking-over date of 1 July 2019, which is 26 days before the accident; the report does not explain how the two fit together. On land, the report says the involuntary resettlement policy was complied with, that land acquisition and resettlement plans were prepared and published for every road package, and that all affected people were paid at replacement cost on the basis of a valuation by a firm outside the project; the rating for social safeguards was raised from Moderately Satisfactory to Satisfactory in December 2018 after early delays. Twenty-four complaints were received and resolved over the life of the project, mainly about environmental and quality shortcomings, the last of them in October 2018.
cases.killed_note: The one death is the site engineer killed on package 21A on 27 July 2019. The completion report gives two things as the cause in the same sentence: human error by the driver of a car that hit him from behind at about 60 kilometres an hour while he stood in the middle of the carriageway taking photographs, and the absence of adequate traffic management provisions, which the report says would have prevented it. The report says the case was handled under the Bank's environmental and social incident response procedure, that the family received the full payment due under Indonesia's work-accident insurance scheme in October 2019, that the highways directorate prepared and carried out a safeguards corrective action plan, and that the Bank closed the case with an after-action memorandum in July 2020. A payment under a work-accident scheme is not a statement of who was at fault.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2021. The completion report lists package 21A as completed. The Bank formally closed the fatality case in July 2020.

cases.point: Kasiglahan Village, Barangay San Jose, Rodriguez (Montalban), Rizal, the site the completion report names as where most of the families were accommodated. Point from OpenStreetMap; the documents give no coordinates for the ecotourism site itself.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P070899. The completion report covers the original loan and the additional financing together and gives no project number for the additional financing; the number P117470 is the one ICIJ files it under. Loan 7205-PH (IBRD-72050) of US$5 million for the Laguna de Bay Institutional Strengthening and Community Participation Project, dated 26 January 2004, approved 4 December 2003, effective 2 April 2004; additional financing of US$10 million as loan 8035-PH (IBRD-80350), approved 12 April 2011, dated 12 May 2011, effective 27 July 2011, of which US$4.5 million was cancelled on 11 July 2013 and a further US$3 million at project closing. The closing date was extended five times: four extensions totalling 27 months, to 30 April 2011, and then a fifth of three years when the additional financing became effective, to 30 April 2014, when the project closed. The Bank's completion report of 25 November 2014 gives the amount disbursed as US$6.80 million on its data sheet and US$6.83 million in its financing table. Environmental category B. The involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12 and the indigenous peoples policy were triggered. The report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory, the government's performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and risk to the development outcome Substantial. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 8 October 2015 agrees on outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance, and prints the risk rating as Significant.

lenders.role: Parallel grant TF-52826 of US$5 million at appraisal for the institutional development component, of which US$4.24 million was spent, per the completion report's financing table.

companies.name: Laguna Lake Development Authority
companies.role: Implementing agency, the national government corporation that regulates the Laguna de Bay basin; it lent project funds on to local governments, which chose and built the sub-projects.

companies.name: Municipal Government of Rodriguez, Rizal
companies.role: The local government that ran the ecotourism sub-project. The Bank's completion report says it had to relocate and resettle the 397 families and that it prepared the resettlement action plan, and that it is leading the building of the Sitio Sapo site with the National Housing Authority on land development.

cases.community: The project lent money to local governments around Laguna de Bay for small environmental works. The Bank's completion report says one sub-project carried a relocation and resettlement requirement: "The Rodriquez LGU had to relocate and resettle 397 families of illegal settlers from their ecotourism sub-project site." Most of those families were accommodated at Kasiglahan Village Phase 1-D in Barangay San Jose. The relocation of a few families was still outstanding when the project closed, because the Sitio Sapo resettlement site had been held up over its development permit and environmental compliance certificate; the report says that site was still under construction, led by the municipality with the National Housing Authority on land development and a non-governmental organisation on social preparation and house building. The report also records one expropriation case filed over the road right of way for the Pangil materials recovery facility sub-project. The Rodriguez sub-projects appear under the additional financing in the report's own list of sub-projects. For the rest of the project the report says all land acquisition was done after securing the consent of the owners affected, through purchase, lease, donation, usufruct or exchange, and it rates compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy satisfactory. The ecotourism site also drew a claim from indigenous people that a religious ritual site of theirs lay inside it; the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples investigated, cleared the sub-project, and the municipality signed an agreement giving the indigenous group 3 per cent of the sub-project's revenue.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 30 April 2014. The Evaluation Group's review of October 2015 lists the relocation of a few families to Sitio Sapo as one of two matters still pending at closure, the other being the Pangil expropriation case. Neither document says how many families were still waiting, and no later document was found that says whether the Sitio Sapo site was finished.

cases.title: Housing demolition for the Chunhu access road came to more than double the plan
cases.place: Chunhu, Fenghua, Ningbo, Zhejiang, China
cases.point: Chunhu, Fenghua district of Ningbo, the town at one end of the Fenghua to Chunhu access road the completion report names. Town centre from OpenStreetMap; the Bank documents give no coordinates.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P106956, loan IBRD-78490 of US$50 million for the Ningbo New Countryside Development Project, approved 25 February 2010, effective 16 July 2010, closed 31 March 2016 with no restructuring; the full US$50 million was disbursed. Environmental category B. Three safeguard policies were triggered: environmental assessment OP 4.01, safety of dams OP 4.37 and involuntary resettlement OP 4.12. The Bank's completion report of 20 October 2016 rates the outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory, borrower performance Satisfactory and risk to the development outcome Moderate. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 13 February 2017 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, one notch lower. Its stated reason has five parts: relevance of objective High, relevance of design Substantial, achievement of the rural wastewater objective Substantial, achievement of the infrastructure objective Substantial, achievement of the objective of enhancing township management in small towns Modest, and efficiency Substantial. The review also rates Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory where the report rates it Satisfactory, and rates risk to the development outcome Substantial, naming risks it says materialised without being identified or mitigated; the report itself puts that risk at Moderate and the review's column for the report prints it as Modest. The review agrees with the report on borrower performance.

companies.name: Ningbo Municipality Development and Reform Commission
companies.role: Implementing agency. The completion report names it as the implementing agency; the Ningbo municipal project management office sat within it, with project implementation units in Fenghua, Ninghai and Yuyao counties. No construction contractor is named in the documents.

companies.name: Fenghua Investment Co., Ltd.
companies.role: The completion report names it as the project implementation unit for the Chunhu Town infrastructure development component, responsible for the design and construction of that infrastructure and for servicing the debt from asset management fees paid by Fenghua City. It is also named as the author of the June 2009 resettlement action plan for the Chunhu small town development sub-project. The Evaluation Group rates its performance Moderately Satisfactory.

cases.community: The loan paid for rural wastewater treatment in 144 villages, a coastal water supply in Fenghua and town infrastructure at Chunhu, including the Fenghua to Chunhu access road. The Bank's completion report says that the permanent land acquisition and the demolition of houses both came out higher than planned. Its table in the social safeguards annex gives the finished figures against the planned ones: 325.63 mu of land permanently acquired against 265.06 planned, a rise the report puts at 24 per cent, and 7,647.6 square metres of housing demolished against 3,479 planned. All of the extra demolition is on the access road component, where 7,647.6 square metres came down against 3,027 planned; the report says the demolition doubled because of unforeseen requirements for that road, and that land first thought to need only temporary occupation had to be bought outright because it was unusable on its own once the parcels next to it had been taken. The report also says a grievance system was set up and no complaints were received over the life of the project, that all property losses were adequately compensated, and that a survey by outside monitors put the per capita net income of affected households at about RMB 58,600 in 2015 against about RMB 40,000 in 2009, with 44 per cent of affected people very satisfied with their living conditions, 50 per cent somewhat satisfied and just under 6 per cent neither satisfied nor dissatisfied.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 31 March 2016. The completion report says the resettlement and the buying of the additional land were carried out satisfactorily in line with the resettlement plan, and that a post-evaluation by the National Research Center for Resettlement found the Bank's social safeguard requirements satisfactorily met. cases.community: Floods on 13 April 2004 killed an estimated 100 people in Djibouti city and affected more than 100,000. The project rebuilt the Ambouli embankment dike and paid for basic services at a resettlement site 12 km out of the city, called PK 12. The completion report's indicator table says 100 per cent of families were resettled, and that this takes in "approx. 240 families affected by the flood and 120 affected by the dike construction and resettled later on". The report's account of the Bank's internal quality review puts it the same way: compensation for "some 120 families living on the reconstruction site, as well as another 240 families who were victims of the flood" had to be settled before the dike could be designed and tendered. The government's own completion report, printed inside the same document, gives different figures. It says the rehousing plan "involves 127 households, of whom 55 are victims of the flooding and 72 have been displaced by the dike reconstruction work". The Bank's text also says that out of 127 families eligible for resettlement at PK 12, 94 took a new house, 2 took a plot and the rest moved elsewhere. In the project's first year the government did not hand occupancy permits to the families moved to PK 12, did not provide their precise numbers or names, and postponed dealing with compensation; the permits were a condition of the credit for delivering latrines and water at the site. The resettlement plan the government filed in July 2006 does carry a named list, of 127 households living in 105 structures affected by the dike construction, with a cut-off date of 2 June 2005. The Bank's team recorded that the government was reluctant to apply the resettlement policy, which it considered too generous towards illegal squatters. At PK 12 the report says the new houses are better than those the flood destroyed and that water standpipes and latrines were provided, but that the families "have difficulty finding jobs, as the resettlement site is far from downtown Djibouti", and that several of the resettled families had made a living from vegetable gardening in the Ambouli river bed. At the last supervision meeting the residents said water supply had failed for the previous two months and that schools and work were far away. The report answers that the distance to the city centre is real but that no land was available for resettlement closer in. It says the resettlement action plan was in the end prepared and implemented in a satisfactory manner, and the evaluation review says all 360 families were given occupancy permits.

The same report's own narrative says 127 families were eligible for resettlement at PK 12, of whom 94 took a house and 2 a plot, which cannot be squared with 360. The government's report, printed inside the completion report, gives 127 households in all, of whom 55 are flood victims and 72 displaced by the dike reconstruction work; that passage is written in the future tense and describes the plan rather than the result. The resettlement plan of 15 July 2006 covers the transfer of 127 households living in 105 structures, all of them for the dike construction. The figure held here is the completion report's 120, the only count the report attaches both to the dike works and to a word meaning moved.

cases.outcome: The dike was finished in March 2009, after the closing date had been pushed back from 30 September 2008. Financing was secured for an upstream dam at Boulle to take pressure off the dike. Of the 400 latrines planned for PK 12, 300 were built; the report says that number is sufficient for the resettled population.

cases.community: The project rebuilt electricity distribution networks in Kigali, in Gasabo District. Under the lender's own rules a resettlement action plan has to be written before works that take land begin, and no civil works are to start until the people affected have been compensated. For the Gasabo distribution lines and four mini substations, the plan was written afterwards. The document is titled "Retrospective Resettlement Action Plan", is dated June 2010, and says plainly: "the report has been prepared after compensation has occurred". Civil works began in November 2007. The plan gives 2.5741 hectares of land to be acquired and 440 people affected by the loss of land, structures, crops or trees, 95 of them through land expropriation. It says there was "already some compensation in form of cash provided to the PAPs following displacement that has occurred". Its own payment annexes show money still owed. For land the grand total is RWF 122,145,102, of which RWF 109,785,402 is marked paid and RWF 12,359,700 "not yet paid". For structures, crops and trees the total to be paid is RWF 94,574,341, of which RWF 88,285,300 is marked paid and RWF 6,289,041 "not yet paid". The same document also states that works began only after all affected people had been identified and compensation provided, and that copies of the cheques can be produced on request. A separate abbreviated plan for the Birembo substation at Kinyinya, in the same district and dated July 2008, records four affected people and says the land acquisition "will lead to the physical displacement of some of the households living in the project site". It names one of them, a widow who it says demolished her mud-walled house and moved to a rented house nearby before compensation reached her, and states that she alone of the four would be given funds to build a new house, the other three being landlords who had rented their dwellings out. The completion report says resettlement and compensation of project-affected people "was completed satisfactorily". The evaluation review carries the same sentence but attributes it to the Bank's project team rather than to a document.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 459 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The retrospective plan counts 440 people affected by the loss of land, structures, crops or trees, in the future tense, and no document counts anyone rehoused. The abbreviated plan for the Birembo substation, dated July 2008, says the land acquisition there will physically displace some of the households on the site and names four affected people without counting anyone moved. The abbreviated plan for the Jabana thermal power plant, of the same month, is the one that says its land acquisition would cause economic and not physical displacement.
cases.outcome: The project closed in 2011 and the completion report rates it Satisfactory. The retrospective plan's annexes leave RWF 18,648,741 of compensation marked as not yet paid as of June 2010, across the two payment tables. No later document in the project's record says whether that money was paid.

cases.community: The project built irrigation dams, diversion weirs and hillside terraces at sites across Rwanda. The completion report counts 2,135 project-affected households, "of which 117 required relocation and were resettled in Project constructed houses". Compensation came to more than RWF 1.41 billion, about US$1.6 million, and 1,288 affected households were offered work during the terracing. The report says households were compensated under Rwanda's expropriation law of 11 June 2015, before civil works began, and that where that law and the lender's policy differed the lender's policy was applied. Two people died during the works. In July 2016 a contractor's worker fell into a spillway foundation pit; the report says that death "was noted as being the result of ineffective safety measures around excavated areas in the site". In November 2017 a boy drowned in a dam reservoir. The worker was insured and his family was paid by both the insurer and the contractor; the drowned boy's family was given money by the ministry for the burial. The project unit then ordered an environmental, health and safety audit of all its dam sites. Fifteen grievance committees recorded eight kinds of complaint. Four were claims against the project: disagreement over the value of resettlement or compensation between an affected person and the independent valuer; inactive or missing bank accounts that delayed compensation; missing land titles that delayed both compensation and construction; and erosion, runoff and dust away from the sites. Four were claims the project treated as unfounded or as matters between neighbours: people who claimed compensation without having been affected; people who claimed for assets acquired after the cut-off date; disputes between neighbours over adjoining plots; and successions, divorces and other family disputes over who owned an asset. The report says all grievances were resolved and that proper records of them are held. The Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats the 2,135 and 117 figures and says compensation and jobs were provided ahead of any civil works; it does not mention either death.

cases.community: The project paid for drainage works in Beira and Maputo and for green urban infrastructure along the Chiveve River in central Beira. The completion report says the works in Beira "recorded recurrent issues of non-compliance with OHS and community health and safety plans" and names the deaths. For the Beira drainage works it counts "the fatality of one worker and three community members", and its footnote gives the causes: a worker hit by a third-party vehicle while moving between work sites; a nine-year-old child who drowned in the retention basin construction site outside working hours; and two people killed in traffic accidents involving the contractor's vehicles. For the green infrastructure works in Beira a second footnote records "a fatality of a 7-year old child who was hit by a contractor's vehicle". Those works' main difficulty, the report says, was the contractor's lack of commitment to community and worker safety and to national employment and labour law, including weekly rest and limits on working hours. The report also names two more deaths it does not attribute to the project: another child found dead in the drainage canals outside the construction sites, and a body found in the Chiveve retention basin during construction. In Beira the project built 21 new houses and 81 latrines for structures the works hit, paid for 498 trees, and compensated 610 people who grew vegetables in small plots known locally as machambas, reaching 98 per cent of them for their crops. In Maputo the report says resettlement "was problematic". The canal's original line would have affected seven houses at a site known as ravines 3 and 4. By the time the plan was being written the number of affected people had risen to 18, and they had already left the land after being paid by a private developer who was buying the land rights from the Municipality of Maputo. The Bank's team could not get clear information from the agency or the municipality and demanded an independent audit. The audit found the money the developer paid "did not meet the requirements of Bank safeguard policies and was not developed in accordance with the applicable Mozambican legislation". It told the project to give a new plot to one affected person who had wanted to be compensated by the municipality instead, to provide land papers to the others, to help those who had lost their source of income, and to pay six months of lost income. The audit was presented in February 2018 and the project reported the fixes done in June 2018, before the works started.
cases.displaced_label: people who had left the ravines 3 and 4 site in Maputo, from the Independent Evaluation Group's review, which says the project-affected people, 18 in total, had already received compensation from a private developer and resettled; the money that moved them came from that developer, which was buying the land rights from the municipality, and not from the credit
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 276 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report says the canal's original line would have affected seven houses and that by the time the plan was prepared the number of affected people had risen to 18; the evaluation review calls the 18 a total of people. In Beira the project built 21 houses for structures the works hit and temporarily moved market vendors, and the documents give no count of the vendors.
cases.killed_note: Five deaths in Beira are recorded with a cause tied to the works or the contractor: a worker hit by a third-party vehicle while moving between work sites, a nine-year-old child who drowned in the retention basin construction site, two people killed in traffic accidents involving the contractor's vehicles, and a seven-year-old child hit by a contractor's vehicle on the green infrastructure works. The documents do not agree on the total. The Independent Evaluation Group's review gives four fatalities, one worker and three community members, and leaves out the seven-year-old. A lessons paragraph in the completion report itself says four fatalities of community members were caused by traffic accidents involving construction vehicles, where its own footnotes give three. Two further deaths are named and are not counted here: another child found dead in the drainage canals outside the construction sites, and a body found in the Chiveve retention basin during construction, which the report says was not shown to be related to the works.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 30 September 2020, almost three years late. The safeguards rating on the municipal grant component fell to Moderately Unsatisfactory in 2016, after a review found that 20 municipalities lacked the capacity to run environmental and social measures on small works, and was back at Moderately Satisfactory by closing. A labour audit finished in October 2020 and an environmental audit in November 2020; by mid-March 2021 the contractor had not produced satisfactory evidence for 11 of the labour audit's corrective actions, 15 per cent of them, and 14 of the environmental audit's measures, 21 per cent, were late. The updated plan for putting market vendors back into the new Chiveve market had been sent to the Bank but could only be carried out after the works were handed to the agency and the municipality in late March or early April 2021, a handover delayed by Cyclone Eloise. The green infrastructure works also had direct impacts on protected mangroves in the Chiveve basin, and restoring them was part of the post-closing plan.

cases.community: The credit paid for road works in Lesotho, including two bridges over the Senqu and Senqunyane rivers and work on two junction roads, Teyateyaneng to Mapoteng and Nyenye to Makhoroana. When the additional financing was added, the report says, the assessment of its safeguards impacts was underestimated and implementation was unsatisfactory: environmental measures were neither systematically monitored nor documented, workers' safety measures "were only respected partially", and further resettlement activities were found later. cases.community: The Raciborz Dolny dry polder was built on the land of two villages, Nieboczowy and Ligota Tworkowska. The completion report of 28 January 2021 says the process "included around 700 individuals belonging to about 250 households", and that "aside from the houses, church, and cemetery, all public facilities needed to be relocated". The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 10 June 2021 gives the same figures: "250 families were resettled, representing about 700 residents". A new village with all services was built for them near Syrynia, about 7 km from the old site. The appraisal document of 21 February 2007 records that the polder needed about 2,600 ha of land, that 20 businesses were in the polder area, most of which would be relocated or closed, and that 22 community assets would be closed or relocated, including a church, a chapel, seven crosses, five wayside shrines, a cemetery, two fire brigade buildings, a kindergarten, a school, a bread house, a recreation room and a sports club. Thirteen wayside shrines and conciliation crosses were moved to the new village. Most houses were bought by agreement over 2003 to 2012: the resettlement plan update of March 2015 counts about 68 buildings acquired by 2006, 1 in 2007, 14 in 2008, 11 in 2009, 8 in 2010, 16 in 2011 and 55 in 2012. In 2013, 30 houses were acquired under an administrative decision of the Silesian Voivodeship of 26 November 2012 rather than by agreement. Opposition was organised and long-running. A Committee for the Defence of Nieboczowy against Displacement was formally constituted in March 2002; the same plan update records 150 appeals against the location permit lodged with the Ministry of Infrastructure and 18 at the Administrative Court in Warsaw, with the Supreme Administrative Court rejecting the complaints on 27 April 2007. A 1998 survey of the two villages found that 91.9 per cent of those surveyed formally accepted displacement; the same plan update records that the survey met hostility and that ten households, 6 per cent, in Nieboczowy refused to answer it. A July 2002 survey of the same population, which followed a campaign by the defence committee urging residents not to co-operate, collected data from 70 per cent of households: 42.2 per cent gave express consent, 8.9 per cent had no opinion and 29.4 per cent refused outright. The same plan update records 74 property owners declaring a will to move in 2007 and 72 families willing to resettle as of April 2010. The completion report says there was "strong initial opposition, even leading to violent resistance", and that the project then built support through consultation; it says the resettled people "have indicated repeatedly that they are content with the new situation", and the Bank presents the resettlement as international best practice. RMF24 reported in April 2007 that about 200 residents were blocking the reservoir and would leave only if the whole village, including the church, was moved with them. The Catholic weekly Gosc Niedzielny reported on 30 June 2020, when the reservoir opened, that Nieboczowy's residents had jointly asked to be relocated and that the new village was built from scratch about 7 km away.

cases.point: Hade village, Obiliq municipality, as OpenStreetMap records it. The Shala neighbourhood was part of Hade. The resettlement site, Shkabaj or New Hade, is about 8 km east, nearer Pristina.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Energy Sector Clean-up and Land Reclamation Project, P096181, grants IDA-H2340 and IDA-H3190 and credit IDA-52400, with trust funds TF-13509 and TF-90160. lenders.role: Co-financier. A grant of US$4.33 million agreed in December 2006 covered the original project's financing gap, and a second grant of US$1.2 million came with the second additional financing (completion report, 28 February 2017).

It operates the Kosovo A and Kosovo B lignite power plants and the mines that supply them; the project was designed in part to build capacity inside it for clean-up and mining operations. Its mine expansion took the land of the Shala neighbourhood, and it paid the compensation and the temporary rent allowances.

companies.role: The ministry responsible for implementing the Shala Resettlement Action Plan, including building the water, sewage and electricity infrastructure at the resettlement site. It ran the grievance commission, which the resettlement completion report says stopped working.

companies.name: rePlan Inc.
companies.role: The international resettlement consultancy commissioned to prepare the Shala Resettlement Action Plan and then, under the Bank-financed Component F, to monitor and report on its implementation.

cases.community: KEK's lignite mine expansion took the Shala neighbourhood of Hade village. The resettlement completion report of July 2016 counts 93 affected households: 63 of them, with 320 full-time residents, were resident households that "needed to be physically displaced", and the other 30 lost land only. By June 2015 the report records 0 of the 63 households still living in Shala. In January 2012, 21 of the 93 households were found to be in a risk zone, were required to leave at once, and were given a monthly rent and living allowance. The Inspection Panel visited the site in 2015 and its Report and Recommendation of 2 September 2015 records residents saying they had been living in temporary housing since 2011 or 2012 because the resettlement site was not ready, and that only in late 2014 did they receive their plots. The same residents told the Panel that the food allowance and emergency rent assistance they had been given during the temporary relocation was discontinued in April 2014 even though the site was not yet ready and many households were still in rented housing. The Panel team recorded its own observations of the incomplete sewerage and the poor condition of the secondary roads at the site. The Bank's completion report says the resettlement was in breach of the Resettlement Action Plan and of the project's legal covenants by December 2013, and that the Bank threatened to suspend disbursements; the breach was resolved when KEK approved more rent payments for the 21 families. The report also records untimely payment of the temporary rent allowances as putting the project in bad standing with its legal covenants. Rebuilding was slow. The resettlement completion report counts 52 of 52 plots allocated with title deeds issued by June 2015, 48 of 52 construction permits issued, 22 plots with construction started or finished, 15 of those 22 houses ready to live in and 12 occupied, with 53 people living at the new site. The same report gives its own explanation for the 30 allocated plots not built on: informal engagements with households revealed that many had opted to stay in the temporary accommodation they had taken in Pristina, while others chose to buy or build elsewhere, and some judged the resettlement site incomplete. Three houses that were ready stood empty in February 2016 because the sewage collecting pipe was blocked. Residents reported 50 metres of blocked sewage pipe in October 2015 and the ministry estimated that about 200 metres needed replacing. Three of the 30 households that lost land only had still not claimed their compensation in February 2016. The 2015 survey ran 32 interviews covering 38 of the 93 affected households, a sample the report puts at 40.8 per cent with a margin of error of 10 points. In it, 43.8 per cent said their economic situation was worse than a year before, against 23.1 per cent in 2011; in the same table the share saying it was better rose from 7.7 per cent to 25 per cent and the share saying it was the same fell from 67.3 to 31.2 per cent. Among the households that lost land without moving, 62.5 per cent said they were worse off, against 37.5 per cent of those physically displaced. The same report concludes that "livelihoods and living conditions have been at least restored and in some instances improved", and that compensation complied with the Bank's resettlement policy. Residents told the Inspection Panel a different story: that compensation was set on a 2004 valuation, that they had to pay the difference between the value of their old plots and the new ones, which they put at about 12,500 euros, that their new plots were smaller, that 20 jobs KEK was to provide under a 2011 agreement had not all materialised, that there was no school or clinic near the site, and that they had never been told of any grievance mechanism.

The resettlement completion report of July 2016 attributes the 93 affected and 63 physically displaced households to the Shala Resettlement Action Plan as of November 2011, and records the outcome in its own indicator table: 0 of the 63 still residing in Shala as of June 2015.

cases.killed_note: No death is recorded in the project documents or the Inspection Panel report.
cases.outcome: The Shala neighbourhood is gone and the mine has expanded over it. The Inspection Panel investigated and its report went to the Bank's board in 2016. The Bank's management agreed to three follow-up actions: repairing a 200-metre section of clogged sewage, technical assistance to revise the resettlement policy framework, and a workshop with the government and KEK. The completion report says the sewage was repaired by December 2016 and the workshop was held on 14 February 2017, and notes that only the sewage repair is directly linked to the project. At the project's closing in August 2016, 12 of the 52 households that chose a plot at the new site were living there. In September 2016 KEK opened negotiations with several hundred more residents who are to be moved for new excavations.

The CEE Bankwatch post of 19 December 2016 is a guest post by Dajana Berisha of the Forum for Civic Initiatives, whom the Requesters designated as their representative to the Panel, so it is a party's account and not an independent one; it gives a third reading of the Panel's finding, that the Bank did not make the resettlement decisions and could not be held directly responsible but could have given specific advice on mitigating the impacts and did not. Prishtina Insight, which saw the leaked investigation report, reported on 14 November 2016 that the Panel found the Bank's management not in compliance with its involuntary resettlement procedures because the resettlement policy framework did not include principles and methods for valuing the assets of people living under the restrictions of the New Mining Field zone, and that the Bank's failings contributed to "real and often severe harm" over a prolonged period. The Independent Evaluation Group's review gives a different account: it says the Panel recognised the Bank's approach and supervision as in compliance, with "two minor instances of non-compliance" over asset valuation, infrastructure delays and malfunctioning sewage, and it sources that statement not to the Panel's report but to management's response to it. The Panel's 2016 investigation report itself was not opened; what was read is the Panel's Report and Recommendation of 2 September 2015, written at the eligibility stage. Both accounts are given here. The lender states that the project did not cause or finance the resettlement and only monitored it, while the resettlement plan it rests on was prepared under a different Bank-financed project. cases.title: A road worker killed and a resident's house damaged on the Igoeti highway works
cases.place: Igoeti village, Kaspi municipality, Shida Kartli, Georgia
cases.point: Igoeti village, Kaspi municipality, as OpenStreetMap records it. The project upgraded the 24 km of the E60 highway from Igoeti to Sveneti and built the Igoeti bypass and its four bridges.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Second East-West Highway Improvement Project, P094044, credits IDA-43730 and IDA-45120. Approved 18 December 2007, closed 30 June 2012. XDR 34.72 million disbursed. The completion report of 28 December 2012 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 28 October 2013.

companies.name: Roads Department of Georgia
companies.role: The national road agency, moved in the 2009 ministerial reforms from the Ministry of Economic Development to the new Ministry of Regional Development and Infrastructure, and the project's implementing agency. Its Resettlement Unit, four staff plus a hired consultant, handled land acquisition and compensation. The completion report does not name the construction contractors, calling them "the first road contractor" and the contractor hired in June 2011.

cases.community: One of the first road contractor's local employees was killed while performing a pavement test on the project section. The completion report of 28 December 2012 says he was "killed by a speeding car whose driver ignored a road construction warning sign", and that the contractor "refused to pay compensation to the victim's family for about 1.5 years, despite constant reminders by the Bank Team" and the Roads Department. The report's lessons section says the accident shows that traffic safety during road construction works remains a problem, and that payment to a contractor should be refused where it has not met safety requirements. The same contractor started civil works before land acquisition from a resident of Igoeti village was officially completed, and in doing so damaged her house and made improper use of her land. That case stayed open from 2009 until 25 June 2012, when she signed an agreement accepting GEL 11,139, about US$6,700, for 954 square metres of land and 62 fruit trees; payment took effect on 9 July 2012. She had already been paid GEL 45,000, about US$27,270, in February 2011 for damage to her summer house during construction. The report says the first contractor's work was unsatisfactory in many instances, that it knew of design errors and "took advantage of the situation", and that it failed to comply with the environmental management plan, especially on storage and disposal of materials. Land take ran well beyond the original plan: the original resettlement plan envisioned 167 land plots covering 91,968 square metres on the Igoeti to Sveneti section, and the number of plots actually affected within the right of way of the main alignment reached 192, covering 146,914 square metres. The completion report attributes the difference to inconsistent right-of-way data and poor coordination between the cadastral data in the plan and the data used in the preliminary design. About 4 more hectares of private land were needed for connecting roads to neighbouring villages. The completion report says all compensation was paid by the end of the project, totalling GEL 1,343,773, about US$0.81 million, and that all outstanding cases were resolved to the satisfaction of the affected people.
cases.killed_note: One local employee of the first road contractor was killed on the project section while performing a pavement test. The completion report of 28 December 2012 says he was "killed by a speeding car whose driver ignored a road construction warning sign", calls it "the fatal accident on the Project section", and draws the lesson that traffic safety during construction works on roads remains a problem and that payment should be refused to a contractor found not to have complied with safety requirements. The cause the document gives ties the death to the works, so it is counted. The worker is not named and the report gives no date for the accident.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 607 for this project. No project document records anyone being relocated: the appraisal document said no physical relocation was expected, and the completion report records land and tree compensation only.
cases.outcome: The highway section is built. The first contractor's contract was allowed to expire and another contractor was hired in June 2011 to finish the works and repair the defective ones. The family of the dead worker was paid after about a year and a half, according to the completion report, which does not give the amount. The Igoeti land case closed with payment in July 2012.

cases.point: Bagdad (Bog'dod) town, Bagdad district, Fergana region, as OpenStreetMap records it. Bagdad is one of the three districts where land was taken; the project area covers about 67,000 ha across the three.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Ferghana Valley Water Resources Management Project Phase I, P110538, credit IDA-46480. Approved 24 September 2009, closed 31 December 2016. XDR 33.76 million disbursed. The safeguards compliance rating was downgraded during implementation over the land acquisition and later upgraded. The completion report of 16 May 2017 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 16 October 2017.

companies.name: Projects Implementation Unit for Water Infrastructure, Ministry of Agriculture and Water Resources of Uzbekistan
companies.role: The unit inside the national water ministry that ran the project, prepared the resettlement plans and the land acquisition reports, and operated the grievance mechanism. Compensation amounts were set by decisions of the Fergana regional governor (khakim) and the district governors.

cases.community: Rehabilitating drainage and irrigation canals took farm land, permanently and temporarily, and removed trees along roads, canals and drains. The resettlement plan prepared before appraisal and updated in 2011 covered 37 farmers. The completion report of 16 May 2017 says that "between 2012 and 2014, 338 farmers were affected by the project activities, and land acquisition took place without the RAP being updated, which constituted a noncompliance with the World Bank OP 4.12", because local authorities would not approve updates until the list of farmers was final. The report also says that "compensation payments were done with delay after land acquisition and/or civil works started", blaming invalid bank details and suspended bank accounts, and that "in most cases, the PAPs did not receive any cash as compensation was used to settle outstanding tax arrears". It adds that some farmers who were paid turned out not to be affected at all, and that there was no mechanism to recover those payments. The borrower's own report on land acquisition in 2012 to 2014, dated November 2015, puts figures to it and explains most of the gaps. Four decisions of the Fergana regional governor between October 2011 and April 2014 covered 513 farm enterprises in all. Under the first, of 10 October 2011, all 37 enterprises listed were paid in full. Under the decision of 13 December 2013, damage to 189 enterprises was assessed at UZS 611,791,000 and UZS 512,663,126 was paid to 155 of them; of the 34 unpaid, 10 had suffered no damage because part of the collector works was dropped at detailed design, and the money for the remaining 24 came back because their bank details were wrong. Under the decision of 15 February 2014, the report's text says damage to 62 enterprises was assessed at UZS 127,215,230 and UZS 126,246,030 was paid to 60 of them, the other two held up by incorrect bank accounts, while the report's own summary table lists 128 enterprises under the same decision with 60 paid; both readings are in the one document. Under the decision of 15 April 2014, the text says UZS 235,988,691 was paid to 121 land users and that of the remaining 38, 28 had suffered no damage during construction and 10 had money returned over bank details, while the summary table gives 123 paid. The table's total is 373 paid of 513, and the report accounts for the 140 difference as 36 farmers awaiting correct banking details and 104 farmers who were not harmed because the work was done before planting and after harvest; the table's own rows sum to 375 rather than 373. A further decision of 25 December 2014 assessed damage of UZS 494,989,548 and the report says no payment had been made under it because funds had to be reallocated. The report puts total damage under the project at UZS 1,918 million, of which UZS 937,803,509 was paid in 2011 to 2014 and UZS 980,473,630 was still to be paid by the end of 2015, a balance that includes the UZS 436.35 million it estimates for 2015 and not only arrears to the farmers already assessed. Land taken ran 515.25 ha in 2012 and 197.49 ha in 2015; for 2013 the report's text gives 358 ha while its table for the same year totals 334.51 ha, and for 2014 it gives 334.52 ha under one contract and a further 226.57 ha under another. The completion report says all outstanding payments were made before the project closed, and that the use of compensation against tax arrears "did not seem to cause any unhappiness in the farmers' community".
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 263 for this project. No project document records anyone being relocated; the figures in the documents count farmers and farm enterprises whose land was taken, not people moved.
cases.killed_note: No death is recorded in the project documents.
cases.outcome: The drainage works were built and the project closed in December 2016 with the outstanding compensation paid, according to the completion report. The Independent Evaluation Group's field-based Project Performance Assessment Report of 29 March 2019 records both sides of the compliance question: its safeguards section says "overall, the project complied with the implementation of safeguards" and that "previous reviews of the safeguards confirmed full compliance", while its assessment of the implementing agency says the project unit was understaffed for environmental and social safeguards, which "partly led to noncompliance with both", and that issues over approval of the resettlement action plan and delays in compensation payments to project-affected people "persisted for some time, causing the downgrade in safeguards performance ratings".

cases.title: Compensation paid two years late at Dartlo, and grievances left two years at Telavi
cases.place: Dartlo village, Tusheti, Akhmeta municipality, Kakheti, Georgia
cases.point: Dartlo village, Akhmeta municipality, as OpenStreetMap records it. Dartlo is one of three sub-project sites where resettlement impacts occurred; the other two are the towns of Telavi and Kvareli, about 70 and 90 km to the south.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Regional Development Project, P126033, loan IBRD-81480. Approved 20 March 2012, closed 31 December 2017. US$60 million committed, US$57.27 million disbursed, of a total project cost of US$72.18 million. The completion report of 18 June 2018 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and Bank performance Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 21 September 2018 also rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory.

companies.name: Municipal Development Fund of Georgia (MDF)
companies.role: The state fund that finances and manages municipal investment works and was the project's implementing agency, with the Ministry of Finance as borrower. It prepared and implemented the abbreviated resettlement plans and ran the grievance mechanism; its safeguards staff grew from 5 to 12 during the project.

companies.name: National Agency for Cultural Heritage Preservation of Georgia
companies.role: The state heritage agency, which cleared designs and developed the second phase sub-project for Dartlo, a protected heritage village (completion report, 18 June 2018).

cases.community: Three sub-projects moved people or interrupted their livelihoods: Dartlo, a protected village high in Tusheti, and the towns of Telavi and Kvareli. The completion report of 18 June 2018 says the Kvareli plan covered temporary income losses of 33 people, the Telavi plan covered temporary relocation and business interruption for 91 households and 84 businesses, and the Dartlo plan covered 44 residential buildings whose owners had to move out for the duration of the works. The same paragraph says both the Kvareli and the Telavi plans "were fully implemented prior to the start of physical works". The resettlement plan update for Dartlo, dated July 2016, records what happened in the first season. Rehabilitation works started on 33 buildings in 2012. All 33 fell in the category whose residents had to move out for the works, but the update records that seven of them were ruins and that seven more had only small-scale works which the building and supervisory company said needed no temporary relocation, leaving the owners of 19 buildings entitled to compensation under the 2012 plan. "In 2012, no one owner of the buildings has received the compensations." Compensation due for 2012 to 21 affected persons was paid in 2014 to 19 of them, and two were still waiting, with payment planned for 2016 once the plan was updated. The same update counts the entitled owners as 19 in one passage and the persons due payment as 21 in another. The update also records that in 2012 none of the buildings was officially registered and owners were identified from villagers' verbal statements, which later changed who was entitled: one building recorded as having a single owner turned out to have three. At Telavi, the completion report says 37 grievances submitted in 2014 were not addressed until 2016. A footnote says those grievances "involved claims by affected business owners that the provided compensation did not fully cover losses incurred as a result of the Project". An independent consultant was appointed in the summer of 2014 to help settle them and to check whether compensation had been paid in line with Bank policy; the report says the assessment helped address the complaints and "confirmed compliance". Separately, the report records that for an extended period environmental supervision and reporting were poor, "creating substantial risks for the livelihood of affected communities, health of workers": construction companies operated without adequate arrangements for waste disposal, and there were "obvious deficiencies in protecting workers' health and safety as well as in managing disturbance of communities residing in and around work sites". The completion report says the project was compliant with the resettlement policy, that all complaints were addressed, and that the Dartlo plan was completed without grievances or complaints.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 165 for this project. No document records a permanent relocation. The counts in the documents are of plan coverage for temporary moves and business interruption: 91 households and 84 businesses at Telavi, 44 residential buildings at Dartlo, 33 people at Kvareli.
cases.killed_note: No death is recorded in the project documents. The completion report records deficiencies in protecting workers' health and safety but no injury count.
cases.outcome: The works are finished and the project closed at the end of 2017. By the July 2016 plan update, two of the Dartlo owners due compensation for 2012 had still not been paid, four years after the works on their houses. The Telavi grievances were settled in 2016 and the lender's assessment found compensation had complied with its policy. No independent account of the Dartlo or Telavi compensation was found.

cases.title: Sixty-five Families Moved from Stilt Houses into Other Stilt Houses in Santos
cases.place: Vila Gilda and the Northwest Zone of Santos, São Paulo, Brazil
cases.point: The Dique Vila Gilda area of Santos, the stilt-house settlement on the Río dos Bugres from which the completion report says the families were moved. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap; the Bank documents give none.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-78070 (7807-BR) for the Santos Municipal Project (P104995), named Santos Municipality in the completion report's own data sheet. US$44.00 million, of which the completion report's data sheet gives US$24.51 million as disbursed and the Independent Evaluation Group's review gives US$24,123,717.34. Borrower the Municipality of Santos, with the guarantee of the Federative Republic of Brazil. Environmental category A. Approved 24 November 2009, effective 19 April 2010, restructured 1 June 2010, mid-term review 12 December 2012, closed 30 June 2015. Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) was triggered. The completion report ICR00003416, dated 7 June 2016 on its cover and carrying 23 September 2015 as the ICR date in its own data sheet, rated the outcome Unsatisfactory, risk to development outcome Substantial, Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, borrower performance Unsatisfactory, quality at entry Unsatisfactory, quality of supervision Moderately Satisfactory, compliance with social safeguards Moderately Unsatisfactory, fiduciary compliance Unsatisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Moderately Unsatisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0020297 recorded the same four main ratings with no disagreement and rated the quality of the completion report Substantial; the review gives the total project cost as US$88 million.

companies.name: Companhia de Habitação da Baixada Santista (COHAB-Santista)
companies.role: The executing agency for resettlement planning, slum upgrading and the move itself, and the builder of the housing complexes the families went to. The completion report describes it as the housing corporation established by the municipalities of Santos, São Vicente, Cubatão and Guarujá and operating under the COHAB By-Laws. It carried out a satisfaction survey of the residents of Vila Pelé II, in 2013 only (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 7 June 2016).

companies.name: Municipality of Santos Secretariat of Government
companies.role: The implementing agency named in the completion report's data sheet. The Secretariat of Government, with support from COHAB-Santos under a specific agreement, took on the institutional responsibilities for resettlement. All resettlement activities were to be paid for out of the municipality's own counterpart funds, not the loan (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 7 June 2016).

cases.community:
The project was meant to clear and upgrade stilt-house settlements on the Río dos Bugres in the northwest of Santos. The appraisal document of 29 October 2009 said about 2,400 families lived in those slums and about 1,100 of them, living in stilt houses, would be resettled into new houses.

By the time the loan closed on 30 June 2015, 712 families had been resettled: 480 to the Vila Pelé II housing complex in 2012, 160 to Caneleira IV Phase 1 in 2014 and 72 to Quadras 1 and 35 in Vila Gilda in 2014. The completion report puts that at 54 per cent of the number estimated in the resettlement action plan. Its resettlement summary table lists 1,324 housing units in total, 712 delivered by the end of the project and 612 still to come, including 520 at Caneleira IV Phase 2 then under construction. A further 88 families, in Vila Gilda, received improved water and sanitation services and adjustments to their housing conditions rather than a move. The project's own indicator was a package of municipal services for 2,400 households; 800 were reached.

In October 2011 the municipality told the Bank it had found 65 more affected families living in the works area, and agreed to pay for temporary housing until they could be moved to new houses, then planned for 2013. At a supervision mission in May 2012 the Bank team found that those families had instead been moved into other stilt houses, built by the municipality, "disregarding the RAP terms and the Bank Policies". The Bank demanded immediate action and the families were moved into temporary housing on housing allowances. The completion report states that by the end of the project "the 65 families, referred above, had not been properly resettled". Annex 4 says around 40 of them reached Caneleira IV Phase 1 late in 2015 and that in May 2016 the municipality confirmed 23 more had finally been resettled, to Caneleira IV Phase 2. Three households were still waiting, with the municipality saying it meant to move them in the second half of 2016. The footnote to the report's resettlement summary table describes a group of the same size and destination differently: "Twenty-three families from Caminho São José (that were receiving rent allowance by EOP) were resettled at Canaleira IV (2nd Phase) in the first half of 2016. The remaining 3 families are supposed to be resettled along the 2nd half of 2016." One account puts the 23 in the group of 65 and the other at Caminho São José, and the report does not say whether they are the same households.

Three expropriation authorisations for the macro-drainage works were still outstanding at closing. The Bank asked in 2015 for an abbreviated resettlement plan for around 30 families occupying pumping station work sites and rejected the one submitted for not complying with its policy; the works were then suspended. A study finished in October 2015, after the project closed, recommended removing the stilt houses within 50 metres of the EEC7 pumping station and within 20 metres of the others. The completion report says the municipality has not yet estimated how many families that is. Geotechnical experts also found that excavation for part of the EEC7 culvert could cause structural damage to nearby buildings.

The completion report records that the 712 families moved from precarious stilt houses into apartment buildings and that the resettlement produced noticeable effects on poverty. None of the Phase I macro-drainage works were finished, so the project achieved little or no flood protection.
cases.displaced_label: families resettled by project closing, from the completion report's resettlement summary table
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ's table carries no displacement estimate for this project. The 712 is the completion report's count of families actually resettled. The appraisal document's 1,100 families is a plan figure, and the 2,400 families and 90,000 residents that appear in both the appraisal document and the evaluation review are counts of the population the project was meant to benefit, not of people moved.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2015 with US$24.51 million of US$44.00 million disbursed. Of the 1,324 housing units in the completion report's table, 612 were still to be delivered after closing. Three households from the group of 65 were still waiting to be moved when the report was written, and the Bank said it was continuing to follow up. The macro-drainage works were suspended, and the Bank told the municipality that all outstanding resettlement and expropriation matters had to be resolved under the resettlement action plan and its safeguard policy before any of the macro-drainage works could continue. Post-occupation surveys reported in the report's economic annex confirm that the resettled population was satisfied with the new condition, and the report records that the 712 families moved into housing complexes with electricity, water supply and wastewater piping. The completion report rated the outcome Unsatisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

Its Chief Engineer was the ministry's representative on the project, responsible for minor civil works and supervision and for defining the project area (Remedial Abbreviated Resettlement Action Plan, 14 March 2013; Resettlement Policy Framework, May 2013).
