cases.community:
The project front-loaded repairs to infrastructure damaged by Hurricane Tomas, which struck in October 2010. The works picked for it were already known to the government and the Bank and were not expected to need any land acquisition, so the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy was not triggered and no resettlement framework or action plan existed.

During work on the Hopewell Road, soil erosion from heavy rainfall in October 2012 forced a change of engineering design, and the new design took land. A survey by the Lands and Surveys Department in September 2012 found encroachment on two properties, one on either side of the road: 3,064 square feet, which the plan puts at 40 per cent of that owner's assets, and 297 square feet, 1 per cent of the other's. Four people, in two families of two, were recorded as directly affected. The Central Planning Division told the Bank on 30 November 2012.

A Bank mission on 5 to 7 December 2012 visited the site, confirmed the encroachment and set out the steps for consulting and compensating the two owners. The same mission found the revised retaining-wall design inadequate, and on 22 December 2012 the Bank told the Director of Planning that the sub-project should be suspended until an acceptable design was produced. The Bank then began a restructuring to trigger the resettlement policy and asked the government to prepare a remedial abbreviated resettlement action plan and a resettlement policy framework.

The remedial plan, dated 14 March 2013, records what was agreed. Both owners chose cash. Compensation for crops was recorded as finalised on 5 March 2013, with values set from Ministry of Agriculture rates; payment for the temporary loss of use of agricultural land and of its productivity had been effected. The two payments for the land itself are recorded as "Awaiting payment", with June 2013 as the expected completion date. The plan's per-person table leaves each land valuation as "value tbd", while its budget table estimates the cost of compensation at XCD 15,570.00 for the 3,361 square feet of land and XCD 5,812.58 for the crops, both to be met by the government out of the Consolidated Fund. The plan notes that there is no provision for land-for-land compensation in the law of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, though it happens in practice case by case. The second owner's private pathway was used as a public right of way while the road was closed; no money was asked for, and instead five street lights were installed along 200 feet of road, officers were assigned from the Mesopotamia Police Station, and the public was urged to respect the property. In consultation the affected people "indicated the need for full and fair compensation of property and crops in a timely manner", and welcomed the gabion baskets supporting their land and crops and the benefit of a stabilised road.

The completion report puts the encroachment at 3,361 square feet in total and says it "did not have a substantial impact on the two affected land owners, nor on the community", and that the Bank, within two weeks of being told, sent a team that helped the government address the consultation and compensation and "effectively address[ed] the problem on the ground". At a second site, the Rillan Hill Community Centre, nearby residents had planted crops before works began; it was decided that no compensation was needed because the crops were harvested first.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 4 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No one was relocated. The remedial resettlement plan records four people directly affected, in two families, each losing part of a plot.
cases.outcome: The credit closed on 31 December 2013 with SDR 3.11 million of SDR 3.30 million disbursed. No document found records the two payments for the land being made; the only figure for them is the plan's budget estimate of XCD 15,570.00. The completion report, six months after the plan's own June 2013 deadline, says the Bank assisted the government in addressing the compensation and that the problem was effectively addressed, but gives no amounts and no date of payment. The remedial plan was disclosed in the country on 12 July 2013 and sent for public disclosure on 16 July 2013, and the project was restructured on 26 August 2013 to trigger the resettlement policy. The mid-term review recommended that the implementation unit's fiduciary and safeguard compliance be strengthened.

cases.community:
The project rebuilt government buildings and infrastructure after the earthquake of 12 January 2010. Resettlement action plans were prepared for five separate works, and the completion report says they resulted in "the relocation of 12 households, land acquisition for 136 households, and non-land economic displacement of 223 households".

The project's social safeguard rating was Satisfactory or Moderately Satisfactory until December 2017, when it was cut to Moderately Unsatisfactory because compensation for land taken from 19 affected people for the Cap Labadie road works had not been paid. They were to have been paid by the government in April 2017. Eight were paid before the scheduled closing date of 29 June 2018. For the remaining 11 the government opened an escrow account at the Banque de la République d'Haïti, provisioned in the amounts set by the government's land acquisition committee, and the accounts are to stay in place for 30 years "to ensure consistency and that obligations can be fulfilled at any time during this period". The resettlement plan for the road was updated and re-disclosed on 25 June 2018, four days before closing, and the project was then closed procedurally. The safeguard rating was put back up to Moderately Satisfactory to reflect the opening of the account.

The June 2018 plan carries the payment record. For the original land acquisitions along the road it says the government paid 5,361,709.80 gourdes to twenty-six affected people, against a February 2015 valuation by the land acquisition committee covering twenty-six affectations and twenty-five people, listed plot by plot with the occupant's name. The nineteen still outstanding are the land taken for the additional works, the slope stabilisation and the outfall canals, which the committee's brigades surveyed between August and December 2017. The plan names the eight paid: cheques were issued for Myrtha Devalsaint, Victor Fadius Francius, Ethma Pierre, Lemercier Etienne, Delaleu Ardouin, Joseph Edwin, Colas Frantz and Regis Jude. It names nine whose expropriation procedures were still being finalised and gives the reason against each: for six, a file left incomplete with documents missing at 20 June 2018; for two, title still being checked by the tax authority; and for Amsterly Pierre, no document at all capable of establishing what he was claiming, after five recorded meetings and letters between October 2017 and 9 June 2018. Two further people were unidentified at 20 June 2018, their plots known only by road position and an estimated 204,000 and 144,000 gourdes. The plan tabulates the escrow sums for the eleven, from 48,060 gourdes to 2,643,300 gourdes, and records that none of the nine was displaced or lost an income-generating activity. For one of the three plots needed for the Ducroix variant the owner asked to be paid in kind, land for land, and the construction plan was changed to avoid the other two plots because their owners could not be found; a design choice made in September 2017 avoided moving one house and its toilet, so those two people were no longer affected.

The project also ran a grievance mechanism with regular open consultations at each site. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that the project team told it that since the report was written 11 of the 19 affected people had been compensated and that the Bank was working with the authorities to compensate the remaining 8. That is a statement by staff rather than a document, and it reverses the split the completion report gives.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 582 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report counts 12 households relocated, land acquisition for 136 households and non-land economic displacement of 223 households across the resettlement plans prepared for five separate works, and assigns none of those figures to a site. No document places any of the 12 relocated households on the Cap-Haïtien to Labadie road, and the June 2018 plan for that road says of the landowners still unpaid that "aucune de ces personnes n'a été déplacées ou privées d'activités génératrices de revenues" — none of them was displaced or deprived of income-generating activities. No count is carried here.
cases.outcome: The grants closed on 29 June 2018, five years after the original closing date, with US$100,526,845 of US$102.8 million disbursed. Eleven of the nineteen people whose land was taken for the Cap Labadie road had not been paid, and their money, from 48,060 to 2,643,300 gourdes a case, sat in an escrow account at the central bank that is to remain available for 30 years. Two of the eleven were still unidentified and for the rest the plan records title documents missing or unverified. The Bank said its implementation support team had taken adequate precautions to bring the pending compensation to a close and that it would keep supervising open cases through other projects run by the same implementation unit. The completion report rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

The indigenous resettlement plan records that one of the two stated grounds for the temporary suspension of works contract No. 487 of 2001, on 22 December 2006, was that this operator had not met its commitment to supply water or to make the missing connections to the pipes already laid, which was one of the undertakings agreed with the community in the consultation meetings (Evaluación Social y Plan de Reasentamiento Indígena, June 2011).

companies.name: Fundación MANA
companies.role: The foundation that prepared the social evaluation and indigenous resettlement plan for the Riohacha wastewater system under Convenio 013 de 2009 with the department (Evaluación Social y Plan de Reasentamiento Indígena, June 2011).

cases.community:
The project built water and sanitation works across La Guajira, a department whose rural population is largely Wayuu. Nine Wayuu communities stood in the direct area of influence of the wastewater treatment lagoons planned for Riohacha: 110 families and 518 people, by the census in the social evaluation and indigenous resettlement plan of June 2011. El Arroyo, La Loma and Campo Alegre were the largest.

Consultation on the lagoons ran for years. The plan records that works contract No. 487 of 2001 was suspended again on 22 December 2006 on two stated grounds: that the water operator had not met its commitment to supply water or complete the missing pipe connections, one of the undertakings agreed with the community, and that the indigenous families settled in the direct area of influence now had to be relocated. In December 2008 two meetings fixed commitments on housing and land purchase and the governor signed an undertaking for the definitive move of the families from the direct area. A list of commitments agreed between 2008 and 2010 includes school classrooms, a school canteen and sanitary units at La Loma, aqueduct pipes for La Loma and Guayabito on relocation, a reservoir, sixteen water tanks across sixteen communities, electricity networks for the relocated sections, a housing subsidy for seven families at Cuatro Bocas, and payment for improvements plus a housing improvement subsidy of up to 5,000,000 pesos each at 2,200,000 pesos a hectare for the land ceded.

The completion report of 15 October 2018 says the indigenous resettlement plan was 96 per cent complete at the time of the report and that the one outstanding commitment for the resettled houses was electrification, for which the government had budgeted but which the project did not deliver. It records that although the project "developed safeguards instruments and carried out consultations in compliance with the policies", it "met significant resistance given that: (i) the municipalities/departments were not complying with the agreements established in the consultations; and (ii) with each consultation, the Project received more demands". The same table records the indigenous peoples plan for the reservoirs as complete and the one for Maicao as 95 per cent complete.

The Riohacha lagoon construction contract was signed in January 2016 and suspended in July 2016 at 9 per cent physical progress, first because of community opposition and then because a new national rule required an archaeological plan, which was approved only at the project's closure. In Maicao the lagoon "was stalled because of complications around the purchase of land for the community members who had to relocate due to the construction of the lagoon. The lagoon was 95% complete when the communities started stalling the works because they had not received any of the benefits agreed on through 'Consulta Previa'/IPP at that time." The land was bought in November 2017 and construction had still not resumed when the report was written. The Maicao lagoons were not financed by the project, which the report says limited the Bank's leverage over safeguard compliance; the project supported the social component there through the indigenous peoples plan.

The department's rural reservoir programme, ten reservoirs in Uribia, was conceived outside the project and brought into it in 2011; the report says it "was not in compliance with Bank safeguards" and that the Bank's team asked for construction to be suspended for want of technical support, and that by the end of the project all the reservoirs were operational and in compliance. The project gave 8,881 Wayuu people improved water sources against a target of 3,500, built ten reservoirs against a target of eight, and cut the time spent fetching water by more than four hours; nine of the ten reservoirs held water fit to drink, and in the tenth, Gran Vía, it did not. Rural sanitation reached 468 Wayuu residents in Riohacha and 112 in Maicao.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 518 for this project. That is to the person the figure in the June 2011 indigenous resettlement plan for the population of the nine Wayuu communities in the direct area of influence of the Riohacha lagoons: 110 families and 518 people. It is a count of people in the affected communities, not a count of people moved. No outcome document found counts the families actually relocated; the completion report refers to "the resettled houses" and says the plan was 96 per cent complete, without a number.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 16 April 2018, six and a half years after the original closing date, with US$71.4 million of US$90 million disbursed. The Riohacha lagoons were 9 per cent built and the contract suspended; the Maicao lagoon was 95 per cent built and stalled. Electrification of the houses the resettled Wayuu families had been given was still outstanding, with the money budgeted by the Temporary Water Administration or the authority in charge. The micro-aqueduct meant to improve water supply to indigenous communities under the Maicao plan stood at 80 per cent. The completion report rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group rated it Moderately Unsatisfactory.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-82890 (8289-EC) for the Manta Public Services Improvement Project (P143996). US$100,000,000, revised to US$99,999,116 and that amount disbursed; the borrower's US$15,600,000 counterpart was revised to zero and none was provided. Borrower the Municipality of Manta with the guarantee of the Republic of Ecuador. Approved 8 August 2013, effective 18 July 2014, mid-term review 11 July 2016, original closing 30 June 2018, actual closing 31 December 2020, after six restructurings. Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.12) was triggered because the water and sanitation works needed permanent and temporary land acquisition. The second-order restructuring of March 2019 required the Regional Vice President's approval, to allow loan proceeds to be spent on land acquisition to compensate sixteen landowners affected by the reconstruction of Vía Barbasquillo; the restructuring of June 2020 reallocated funds between disbursement categories "to complete compensation payments due to land acquisition". The completion report, dated 30 November 2021, rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, monitoring and evaluation Modest, and social safeguards Moderately Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0022845 gave the same ratings and rated the quality of the completion report Substantial.

companies.name: Gobierno Autónomo Descentralizado Municipal del Cantón Manta
companies.role: The municipality that borrowed and implemented, through a project implementation unit that had one social specialist and, the completion report says, low capacity. The report records that the unit's legal team, which prepared the resolutions and carried out the land acquisition, feared future problems with the Comptroller if it followed the Bank's resettlement policy instead of national law, so it "tended to delay decision making, did not implement agreements, and avoided compliance with OP 4.12". It had never run a project financed by a multilateral bank. The municipality had three different mayors and the unit four different leaders over the project's life, and the report records difficulties caused by political actors who wanted to manipulate the project's procurement (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 November 2021).

The completion report quotes its general manager on the effect of the loan on service quality and reports that the project updated and brought into operation the company's commercial system (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 November 2021).

cases.community:
The project rebuilt water, sewerage and street infrastructure in Manta, on the coast of Manabí, which was hit by a magnitude 7.8 earthquake in April 2016.

The Bank's resettlement policy was triggered because the works needed land, permanently and temporarily. The implementation unit prepared a resettlement policy framework in 2016 to deal with people losing access to land, assets or income. The completion report states what happened next: "The PIU's low capacity as well as a high-level of political involvement in the Project contributed to issues with the initial land acquisition processes. Several properties were taken without having all the required permits or without having reached agreements with the owners. This situation occurred for almost a year at the beginning of the Project; the Bank presented its non-conformities in different documents, and the Borrower satisfactorily complied with the required processes."

In March 2019 the Bank restructured the loan, with the approval of its Regional Vice President, so that loan money could be used to compensate sixteen landowners whose land was taken for the reconstruction of Vía Barbasquillo. In June 2020, six months before the loan closed, a further restructuring moved money between disbursement categories "to complete compensation payments due to land acquisition".

The completion report's lessons set out why the compensation went wrong. Ecuadorian regulation "does not reach the full replacement cost required by OP 4.12 for land acquisition". The implementation unit was reluctant to go against national rules even though the Bank's rules take precedence in this kind of project, and its legal team was afraid of trouble with the Comptroller if it followed the Bank's policy, so it delayed decisions, did not implement agreements and avoided complying with the policy. The Bank "had to escalate this issue to the highest level of management to bring about change and ensure compliance", and an agreement signed with the Comptroller proved useful in getting compliance.

The report says the project finished in compliance with all the requirements of the Bank's Environmental and Social Framework despite these difficulties. The project's rehabilitation works benefited 15,740 household sewerage connections, beating the restructured target of 15,500 by 2 per cent and missing the original target of 17,318 by 9 per cent.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 150 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No document found counts anyone relocated. The only figures are the sixteen landowners whose land was taken for the Vía Barbasquillo reconstruction and the "several properties" the completion report says were taken without the required permits or without agreement with the owners.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 31 December 2020, two and a half years after the original date, with almost all of the US$100 million disbursed. Compensation payments for land acquisition were still being completed six months before closing, and the completion report says the project finished in compliance with the Bank's social requirements, with a social safeguard rating of Moderately Satisfactory. The report's own lesson is that projects in countries whose national rules fall short of replacement cost should carry a separate budget line for land acquisition and resettlement from the start. The completion report rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-42470 (4247-BO) and IDA-51680 (5168-BO) for the Bolivia Urban Infrastructure Project (P083979). US$54,000,000 in all, US$30,000,000 under the first credit and US$24,000,000 under the additional financing, of which US$46,218,927 was disbursed. Borrower the Plurinational State of Bolivia. Approved 21 November 2006, effective 12 September 2007, mid-term review 25 September 2009, original closing 30 November 2010, actual closing 30 September 2017, after restructurings beginning 15 August 2010. Component 1 upgraded neighbourhoods in La Paz, Component 2 urban transport in El Alto and Component 3 sewerage in Santa Cruz. Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01) and Physical Cultural Resources (OP/BP 4.11) were triggered; the appraisal document said no resettlement was expected but that works under Components 1 and 2 might in very limited cases entail population displacement. The completion report, dated 26 March 2018, rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Modest, and rated compliance with environmental safeguards Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0021219 gave the same ratings with no disagreement recorded and rated the quality of the completion report Substantial.

companies.name: Gobierno Autónomo Municipal de El Alto
companies.role: The municipality that carried out the El Alto urban transport component. The completion report records that it prepared a conflict management plan and said that documentation of a "voluntary cession of land" had been planned before the project identification phase but was carried out after the Bank became involved, and that it then prepared an abbreviated resettlement plan for retroactive, in-kind compensation. It is left in charge of the one case unresolved at closing (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 March 2018).

companies.name: Gobierno Autónomo Municipal de La Paz
companies.role: The municipality that ran the neighbourhood upgrading component under its Programa Barrios de Verdad. The completion report records that all adverse impacts on third parties in La Paz were dealt with by changes in design, repositioning front walls and small structures such as stairs at the entrances of houses, and that the city prepared an abbreviated resettlement plan establishing in-kind replacement of perimeter walls, entrance stairs and railings (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 March 2018).

cases.community:
The project paved avenues in El Alto, upgraded poor neighbourhoods in La Paz and extended sewerage in Santa Cruz.

On the El Alto avenues the land had already been handed over before the Bank arrived. The completion report says the municipality "prepared a Conflict Management Plan and indicated that documentation of a 'voluntary cession of land' had been planned before the PP's identification phase, but had been carried out after the Bank's involvement in project identification". The municipality then prepared an abbreviated resettlement plan "to provide retroactive, in-kind compensation to 6 property owners for the land they had ceded for the construction of 'Av. Santa Vera Cruz - Tramo 1'. Five of the six cases were solved at the end of the Project, and property owners obtained legal titles for their lots (with their new square footage). Only one case is pending", left with the El Alto municipal government, which expected to finish it within a couple of months.

The retroactive plan for Avenida Litoral, dated 10 November 2010, describes the same pattern on another avenue. Eleven residents of the Urbanización El Paraíso, named one by one in the plan, ceded the land needed for a road line of 48.5 metres, which the municipality had fixed in 2003, two years before the Bank's first identification mission in April 2005. The municipality had itself given up part of the municipal right of way, reducing the line from the 60 metres the law set for a first-order road to 48.5 metres, to avoid expropriating more of the residents' plots; even at 48.5 metres the plots were still encroaching on the right of way by an average of 11.5 square metres. All eleven plots were partially affected and none wholly, and the plan's table of affected assets carries the note that no valuation is made because the transfer is a return of municipal land. Two further signatories of the 2003 agreement, in block M, were held not to be affected at all, because their plans had been approved respecting the 48.5-metre line, so what they had declared as voluntarily ceded was in the plan's words a return of municipal property they had encroached on. Because the areas ceded came to more than 10 per cent of each plot, the Bank's policy required retroactive compensation, and the plan says the Bank was examining whether the 2003 agreement had legal force, whether its signatories were still the owners, and whether they still agreed with what they had signed, since "the areas ceded by the residents are greater than 10%, which may imply an impact of great magnitude for the owners". Of the eleven signatories, the plan notes, one had died, one was a new owner, and for one the original title documents were missing and that owner's willingness to sign the updated agreement had still to be established. The municipality's own position in the same plan is that the safeguards were not triggered, because its legal acts with third parties predate its commitments to the Bank; it would nonetheless make "some compensations" to the eleven, in the form of legalising their title and improving their basic services, and the plan's schedule prices those at 40,876.11 bolivianos in all.

The abbreviated resettlement plan for Avenida Santa Vera Cruz, dated July 2013, counted 137 properties built over the municipal line. One hundred and twenty-eight of them encroached on part of the pavement without blocking it and were not treated as affected; nine blocked the pavement and part of the carriageway and had to pull back to the line. One of the nine owners waived the entitlement and said he would move back at his own expense, leaving eight eligible. In every case the loss was partial and nobody had to move elsewhere. The plan also counted the trades along the avenue: 44 shops selling building materials and daily food, and 54 vehicles belonging to hauliers carrying sand, stone and building materials. Neither group was to get any material compensation. The shops were promised crossings so customers could still reach them; the hauliers were promised help in moving to a nearby part of the avenue where they could work in much the same way.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 148 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No document found counts anyone relocated, and both plans say the impacts were partial and that no one had to move to another site. The completion report counts six property owners given retroactive compensation on Avenida Santa Vera Cruz Tramo 1, of whom five were settled and one was not; the July 2013 plan for the same avenue counts eight eligible affected properties out of nine required to pull back to the municipal line, and the November 2010 plan for Avenida Litoral counts eleven. Neither document explains the difference between six and eight.
cases.outcome: The credits closed on 30 September 2017, nearly seven years after the original closing date, with US$46.2 million of US$54 million disbursed. Five of the six owners on Avenida Santa Vera Cruz Tramo 1 had been compensated in kind and held legal title to their plots at their new size. One case was unresolved and left with the El Alto municipal government, which expected to close it within a couple of months. The completion report credits a community development strategy and a grievance redress service in El Alto with building a stable relationship between the project agencies and the residents and with the successful execution of the resettlement plan. The completion report rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

cases.title: Seven Killed and Ninety-nine Properties Hit When the Pinheiros Station Works Collapsed
cases.place: Rua Gilberto Sabino, Rua Capri, Rua Conselheiro Pereira Pinto, Rua Eugênio de Medeiros and Rua Amaro Cavalheiro, beside the Pinheiros station works on Metro Line 4, São Paulo, Brazil
cases.point: Rua Capri, Pinheiros, one of the five streets the resettlement plan lists, holding 30 of the 99 affected properties, beside the Pinheiros station site. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap; the plan gives street names and no coordinates.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: The works where the ground collapsed were the civil works of Phase 1 of São Paulo Metro Line 4, which the Bank financed. The completion report for the Line 5 project, dated 22 June 2021, lists among the Bank's prior operations in the metropolitan region "the Metro Line 4 Phase 1 Project (P051696), approved in 2002", says those operations supported "construction of Phase 1 of Line 4", and records that "Line 4 Phase 1 was financed under World Bank procurement guidelines". That is the opposite of the arrangement on Line 5, whose appraisal document says the civil works "will be financed and executed by the Borrower" and that construction accident risk "is an indirect risk because Bank is not involved in the civil works". The resettlement plan for the accident is disclosed in the Bank's document archive as RP591, filed under the São Paulo Metro Line 4 Project Additional Financing (P105959), whose approval ICIJ's table records as 8 April 2008, fifteen months after the collapse; the archive files the additional financing's own project paper of 3 March 2008 under both that number and P051696. No completion report and no evaluation review filed under the additional financing number could be reached, and no Bank document found for it states a loan number or an amount. The appraisal document for the São Paulo Metro Line 5 Project (P116170), dated 3 March 2010, records that the State of São Paulo had been managing Metro Line 4 Phases 1 and 2 as a Bank Category A project requiring Environmental Assessment and Involuntary Resettlement policies, that "during project implementation of Line 4 (Phase 1) in January 2007, an accident occurred in which 7 people died due to the collapse of the tunnel at Pinheiros station which was being excavated", and that this "led to additional involuntary resettlement due to damage to homes and to the need to evacuate other dwellings and businesses until their safety could be assured". The same document says the Bank reviewed the design and implementation of the required resettlement and found it satisfactory, and that "the resettlement and compensation of affected parties is now complete, with no cases pending". It also lists the lessons of the Pinheiros accident among the measures to be taken into account on Line 5.

companies.name: Consórcio Via Amarela
companies.role: The consortium carrying out the Line 4 civil works at the Pinheiros station site when the ground collapsed. The resettlement plan says the people and families affected by the accident continued to be dealt with by this consortium and by the São Paulo Metrô, and that the consortium reported the dates on which displaced residents left their hotels or other lodgings (Plano de Reassentamento, December 2007).

companies.name: Companhia do Metropolitano de São Paulo (Metrô)
companies.role: The state metro company building Line 4-Amarela, which ran the census of the affected population and the monitoring visits to resettled households, and which the São Paulo state court ordered to be reimbursed R$6.5 million, the value of the contract, in the improbity judgment published on 16 February 2024 (Plano de Reassentamento, December 2007; Tribunal de Justiça de São Paulo notice, 16 February 2024).

companies.name: Prefeitura Municipal de São Paulo
companies.role: The city government, whose structural reports on the damaged buildings decided which of them could be reoccupied. The plan's table of property conditions distinguishes 34 properties released with a city report, 10 released with reservations, 11 released quickly as minimal impact and 3 with no city intervention (Plano de Reassentamento, December 2007).

cases.community:
On 12 January 2007 the ground gave way at the works for the future Pinheiros station of Line 4-Amarela of the São Paulo metro. Seven people were killed. A resettlement plan setting out the position as at 31 October 2007, published in December 2007 by the metro company and disclosed in the World Bank's archive as RP591 under the Line 4 additional financing, records what the accident did to the neighbourhood. The plan itself names no lender.

Ninety-nine properties were affected, on five streets: 42 on Rua Gilberto Sabino, 30 on Rua Capri, 18 on Rua Conselheiro Pereira Pinto, 7 on Rua Eugênio de Medeiros and 2 on Rua Amaro Cavalheiro. Fifty-eight were residential, 25 commercial, 6 mixed with work carried on at home, 9 unoccupied and 1 other. Twelve were condemned and six demolished; six were sealed off, 17 were still under analysis, 34 were released with a city structural report, 10 released with reservations, 11 released quickly as minimal impact and 3 had no city intervention.

Two hundred and seventy-one people were affected, not counting the owners who did not live in the properties, of whom there were 57. The census counted 134 women and 137 men, 42 people over 65, 52 with chronic illness and 2 with disabilities. Forty-three of the households were tenants paying rent, 10 occupied properties lent to them, 36 were resident owners and one entry is recorded as squatters.

Seven deaths are recorded. Eight indemnity agreements were signed for them, because in one case the victim had two families.

Of the 99 properties, nine were empty on the day of the accident and four stayed occupied with minimal impact. Eighty cases had been settled by 31 October 2007, producing 34 returns to the original property, 59 resettlement addresses and 8 atypical cases with neither a return nor a resettlement; the plan notes that some occupants split between several addresses after resettlement. Six cases were still awaiting negotiation: three families lodged only in hotels, one split between a hotel and a relative's house, and two lodged with relatives with their cases in litigation. The hotels used were the George V, the Golden Tower and the New Citi. By the end of October 2007, 103 agreements had been signed out of 147 cases, three of them that month, with 30.67 per cent of those affected back in their own property and 53.15 per cent moved to another; the plan notes that one case can produce more than one agreement. The agreements signed covered indemnity for death, moral and material damages, material damages, damages for the dissolution of a tenancy, lost profits together with moral and material damages, lost profits with other indemnities, and other indemnities.

On 16 February 2024 the São Paulo state court published a first-instance decision in case 0009559-70.2010.8.26.0053, given by the 5th Public Treasury Court of the state capital, holding six people and seven companies liable for administrative improbity over the collapse. The six lost any public office they held, had their political rights suspended for five years, were fined at twice the damage, which is to be quantified later, and were barred for five years from contracting with the public sector or receiving public benefits or tax incentives; the seven companies were fined on the same basis and barred on the same terms. The court ordered the defendants to reimburse the São Paulo Metrô R$6.5 million, the value of the contract, along with what it had spent on indemnities, legal fees and costs, and to pay R$232 million in collective moral damages and R$1.2 million in diffuse property damages. On causation the judge wrote that "as perfurações foram executadas no local já fragilizado, e os suportes de sustentação previstos não foram colocados de imediato" — the drilling was done at a spot already weakened and the planned supports were not put in at once — and found the conduct negligent and the site plainly exposed to imminent risk of collapse, the drilling having been done to get ahead of schedule. He found that representatives of the Metrô had abandoned their duty to supervise and that the consortium's experts had taken no immediate or deeper analysis of the instability they knew of. The decision can be appealed. The court's notice names neither the individuals nor the companies.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 129 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The resettlement plan counts 271 people affected, excluding 57 owners who did not live in the properties, across 99 properties. Its summary gives 59 resettlement addresses out of 80 settled cases, alongside 34 returns to the original property and 8 atypical cases, and notes that some occupants split between several addresses after resettlement, so the 59 cannot be read as a count of 59 households. No figure is carried here as a count of households relocated.
cases.outcome: The resettlement plan's position at 31 October 2007 was 80 of 99 cases settled and six still in negotiation, two of those in litigation. The appraisal document for Line 5, dated 3 March 2010, says the resettlement and compensation of the affected parties was complete with no cases pending, and that the Bank had reviewed the design and implementation of the resettlement and found it satisfactory. The São Paulo state court's improbity judgment of February 2024, seventeen years after the collapse, holds six people and seven companies liable, orders R$6.5 million reimbursed to the metro company, R$232 million in collective moral damages and R$1.2 million in diffuse property damages, and leaves the civil fines of twice the damage to be quantified later; it is subject to appeal.

cases.place: Jhelum Valley Road, Muzaffarabad, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, and National Highways N-15 and N-35 in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
cases.point: Muzaffarabad, the city the Jhelum Valley Road runs from, named in the completion report as one of the three roads rebuilt under this loan. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap's Nominatim search for Muzaffarabad.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: First Additional Financing to the Highways Rehabilitation Project, project number P099040, a US$100.0 million loan (Ln. 7341-PK) approved on 1 December 2005, after the 8 October 2005 earthquake, to reconstruct about 44 km of National Highway N-15 (the Kaghan Valley Road), rehabilitate about 25 km of National Highway N-35 (the Karakoram Highway) and rehabilitate about 59 km of the Jhelum Valley Road in Azad Jammu and Kashmir, and to pay for relocation of utilities, resettlement and land acquisition (Implementation Completion and Results Report, report no. ICR2723, 21 November 2013, section 1.6.1 and section 1.7.1(a)). The loan was one of four financings of a single operation carried under the parent project number P010556, which closed on 30 June 2013. That completion report rates the project's social safeguards Moderately Satisfactory (section 2.4.2) and its overall outcome Satisfactory; the Bank's Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, because efficiency was modest given significant cost overruns (ICR Review, 11 June 2014). The completion report says the Bank financed the land acquisition itself (Annex 7, p. 49).

cases.community: Rebuilding the three earthquake-damaged highways to national standards needed land. The completion report records about 1,007 kanals acquired for the Earthquake Damaged Roads component, valued at about Rs 108 million (US$1.1 million). Of that, Rs 76.5 million (US$0.78 million), 72 per cent, was paid to project-affected people. The remaining Rs 31 million (US$0.32 million) was not paid. The report gives four reasons: some owners died in the earthquake; some left the disaster areas for other parts of the country and could not be traced; some claims are disputed in court; and some are shamlat cases, land with many joint owners whose individual entitlements come to less than US$100 and who are unwilling to open a bank account to receive them. The report says the court cases are unlikely to be resolved in the near future, and that the money is already deposited and held in escrow accounts with the Land Revenue Departments, so compensation will eventually be paid when the cases settle. The Bank's Independent Evaluation Group adds that the project team put the disputed claims at US$0.11 million, 36 per cent of the unpaid balance. The completion report's borrower section records that the Azad Jammu and Kashmir government used land acquisition funds for other purposes rather than disbursing them to affected people, and that the land acquisition was delayed, in the borrower's words, beyond proportion to the extent of risking the suspension of disbursement. At appraisal in 2003, before the earthquake component was added, the project expected to take 6 hectares of land and affect about 350 people. On the main N-5 corridor the works stayed inside the existing right of way apart from five acres at Mitiari bypass, bought by private negotiation at market rates.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2013. About Rs 31 million of compensation was still unpaid, held in escrow by the revenue departments of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Azad Jammu and Kashmir, with the court cases behind part of it expected to take years. No later document showing the money paid out was found.

companies.role: The state body that built the dry port, under Nepal's Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies, which the completion report names as an implementing agency. It ran the grievance notices the requesters answered.

cases.community: The depot was built on land at Chobhar, in Kirtipur Municipality south of Kathmandu, that the state had acquired decades earlier for the Himal Cement Factory, closed in 2002. Residents, mainly indigenous Newars, said the land should go back to its original owners and that disputes over that old acquisition were never settled. The Kathmandu Post reported on 18 January 2019 that the government said it had acquired 1,054 ropanis from the former factory, 228 ropanis of it for the dry port and 826 for an international exhibition centre, and quoted Panchha Lal Maharjan of the Chobhar Conservation Committee saying the government had not acquired all the private land, had not paid 416 former cement factory workers for 19 months, and had not compensated people whose houses were destroyed when the factory was built. The Board's Rabi Shankar Sainju said an audit showed no employee liabilities but that the Board would raise it with the Finance Ministry if the claim was genuine. Local groups stopped the depot works from August 2018 to January 2019, and the Bank told the government it would make no disbursement against the component until community grievances were addressed and the grievance process documented. A two-tier grievance mechanism was then set up, with a committee at the site and one at the ministry.
cases.suppression: Nepal's Prime Minister laid the foundation stone for the dry port on 17 January 2019. The Kathmandu Post reported the next day that around 150 locals had gathered from the morning and that police arrested at least 54 of them, on figures given by the Chobhar Conservation Committee's coordinator. The Request for Inspection later filed with the World Bank's Inspection Panel says fifty-two locals were detained from the streets and from their houses, that the event took place under an undeclared curfew in the construction area, and that construction has gone on behind Armed Police Force guards. The two accounts differ on the number detained, 52 against at least 54.
cases.outcome: The Inspection Panel registered the request on 27 May 2020. After visiting the site and meeting the requesters, the Panel found no sufficient grounds to investigate the complaint, and recommended that consultations with local communities be strengthened in future projects. The Bank told the Panel that several of the complaints concerned actions long predating its involvement, such as land claims going back to the 1960s, and that these were outside the policy's scope. The Bank also said the project recognised the Newars as indigenous peoples and that the policy did not require a separate Indigenous Peoples Plan. Disbursements for the dry port resumed in February 2020. The project closed on 30 November 2021. The requesters say their demand for the return of the land has not been acted on.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 414 for the project as a whole, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Request for Inspection quotes the project's draft environmental impact assessment as stating that all the dry port land is under the ownership of the Government of Nepal and that no further acquisition of land is required, so there is no issue of land acquisition, resettlement or compensation for the project. That assessment is not among the documents cited here; the quotation is the requesters', and they dispute what it says.

cases.title: Households and market vendors moved for heritage works in Tripoli, Tyre and Saida

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Additional Financing for the Cultural Heritage and Urban Development Project, project number P116197, loan IBRD-81370, US$27.0 million, approved 12 April 2012, with effectiveness delayed by a hung parliament. It topped up the original project, number P050529, loan IBRD-71660, US$31.5 million, approved 17 April 2003. One completion report covers both, dated 15 June 2017, and the operation closed on 31 December 2016. The additional loan paid for the later batches of the same works in the same five cities, Baalbeck, Byblos, Saida, Tripoli and Tyre. Its Bank financing was allocated US$17.9 million to rehabilitation of historic city centres and urban infrastructure, US$6.7 million to archaeological sites and US$2.2 million to institutional strengthening (completion report, Annex 1, project financing by component, additional financing). The completion report rates the outcome Satisfactory and safeguards Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, assessing efficiency as modest because of high cost overruns (ICR Review, 22 November 2017). The Bank's Independent Evaluation Group also published a field-based Project Performance Assessment Report on 13 August 2019.

companies.name: Council for Development and Reconstruction of the Republic of Lebanon
companies.role: Implementing agency named in the completion report. A public body reporting to the Lebanese Council of Ministers that contracts and supervises state infrastructure works; two staff of the Directorate General of Antiquities worked full time on its premises to handle archaeological finds. No construction contractor is named in the documents.

cases.community: The works involved involuntary resettlement affecting 760 project-affected people across Tripoli, Tyre and Saida. Six resettlement action plans were prepared. The completion report's own table records what happened: 38 households with 209 people physically relocated from Khan el Askar blocks A and B in Tripoli; 33 households with 124 people physically relocated from Khan el Askar block C; 280 vendors recorded as physically relocated into the new marketplace in Tripoli, the same figure a 2011 project document had already used for the vendors the revised Tripoli plan covered; 3 tenants temporarily relocated from the Salameh building in Saida; and 144 vendors temporarily relocated for the new marketplace in Tyre. A sixth plan, for the physical relocation of 31 people from small shops and warehouses at Khan el-Askar, was never implemented because that component was cancelled. The Tripoli marketplace works were halted for four years from 2012 by active shooting in the city, the census of affected people had to be redone, and that plan was finished three months after the project closed. The Bank's field assessment, published in 2019, found that in the rebuilt covered market in Tyre the expected gains had not arrived: on the day of the visit the market was deserted and the vegetable and fruit sellers were playing cards for want of customers. Interviews recorded fewer permanent vendors working in the market than the resettlement plan had arranged for, fruit and vegetable sellers undercut by traders outside the market who pay no fees, and parking cut to 36 spaces where vendors had been told there would be 180. The market association collected the signatures of hundreds of vendors opposed to the changes and organised two sit-ins. In Tripoli, residents of the historic souk houses told the assessment team they had not been contacted before or during the works and had gone to the engineers on site themselves. Shop owners and tenants in the old souks said they were consulted and promised their objections would be considered, and felt that did not happen. Against this, the completion report says all six plans were financed by the project, four were satisfactorily implemented by closing, the Tripoli plan was satisfactorily implemented by the time of the report, and the new Tripoli marketplace won the Bank's 2017 Sustainable Development Vice-Presidency award.
cases.outcome: The operation closed on 31 December 2016 and the Tripoli marketplace resettlement finished three months later. The Bank's own field assessment of 2019 found the Tyre market underused and traditional businesses around the new public square losing trade, with owners saying the area was being turned over to tourism.
cases.displaced_label: households, physically relocated from Khan el Askar in Tripoli: the sum of the two rows of the completion report's Table 8 that record physical relocation of residents, 38 households with 209 people from blocks A and B and 33 households with 124 people from block C (completion report of 15 June 2017). Separately the same table records 280 vendors physically relocated into the new Tripoli marketplace, and temporary relocation of 3 tenants in Saida and 144 vendors in Tyre.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 371 for the additional financing, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report's own total of people affected is 760 across the whole operation.

cases.community: The completion report records that in Nagapattinam district, work to improve the North Buckingham canal ran ahead of the state's resettlement and rehabilitation policy: the local authorities demolished the affected structures without offering compensation and assistance. After the Bank's team learned of it, the Government of Tamil Nadu drew up retrofit measures and put them in place, and all six displaced families were offered cash grants for the impacts they had suffered. Five families had received the grant when the credit closed on 31 December 2011 and the state was still in the process of paying the sixth. For the resettlement sites as a whole, 560 hectares of land was acquired, 330 hectares of it private land, bought by private negotiation under a special government order letting district collectors set compensation at up to 200 per cent of guideline or registered values; about 40 hectares was donated by local citizens. The completion report says state funds, not Bank funds, paid for that land. The Independent Evaluation Group records that the project team told it the project was in compliance with the resettlement policy at the time the completion report was written, and that the 100 families physically displaced in Tamil Nadu were either given alternative housing or were expected to be shortly; that is a statement by Bank staff, not a document.

The completion report presents this as a gain: compensating squatters rather than only landlords was new in Iraq, the poorest traders benefited, and vendors were able to expand their premises at the new location, with better access and parking. On the new Girsheen-Suheila road corridor in the north, land had to be acquired, and the plan covered the amount of farmland taken, crop loss, who was eligible, the rates for crops and fixed assets, and extra help for three affected people below the poverty line. cases.title: Nearly half the compensation unpaid on the Kabeli corridor transmission line
cases.place: Kabeli corridor 132 kV transmission line, Jhapa, Ilam and Panchthar districts, eastern Nepal
cases.point: Phidim, Panchthar district, on the line's second and third sections and the town where the route had to be changed after local protest. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap's Nominatim search for Phidim, Nepal.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Kabeli Transmission Project, project number P112893, credit IDA-49320 and grant IDA-H6760, approved 10 May 2011, effective 21 September 2011, closing extended by 18 months from 30 June 2015 to 31 December 2016. Component 1, at US$31.56 million, paid for a 90 km 132 kV double circuit transmission line and three new 132/33 kV substations in the Godak, Phidim and Amarpur areas; the completion report records that the fourth substation on the project, at Damak, was financed by the utility from its own resources. The completion report of 12 September 2018 rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory and risk to development outcome High; the Independent Evaluation Group concurs on the outcome, rating it Moderately Unsatisfactory (ICR Review, 14 January 2019). The Evaluation Group's review says social safeguards were only partially implemented and that 55 per cent of compensation for project-affected families was paid.

companies.name: Nepal Electricity Authority
companies.role: Implementing agency named in the completion report. The state-owned utility that generates, transmits and distributes electricity in Nepal; it acquired the land and pays the compensation, and the report says preparation of its resettlement action plan was delayed and the issue was raised repeatedly with its management. Its Deputy Managing Director was handling the two unpaid categories. The Alternative Energy Promotion Centre implemented the rural energy component. No construction contractor is named in the documents.

cases.community: The line runs for 90 km through hill districts of eastern Nepal and needed tower pads, a right of way and the removal of structures. About twenty months after the project closed, the completion report of September 2018 printed the state of the payments, under a heading saying there had been good progress in compensation payment since the closing. For tower pads, 188 of 228 affected families had been paid, 82 per cent; the gaps are owners with no legal title, families unable to produce legal documents, and families unwilling to accept the compensation. For structures, 41 of 82 families had been paid, 50 per cent; three families received only half because they had not yet demolished their structures, one was not paid because the landowner was absent, and 37 structures had only recently been identified and were still being valued. For the right-of-way easement fee, 673 of 1,339 affected families had been paid, 50 per cent; the gaps are difficulty identifying owners and users because the district land survey offices have no record, payments left uncollected because the amount is too small to bother with, and absentees. Resettlement and rehabilitation assistance to the owners of residential structures had still not been paid, which the report attributes to a change in senior management, and assistance to people without title had not been paid because the chief district officer was unwilling to carry out the valuation. A community school in the right of way was being rebuilt, with completion expected by the end of December 2018. Land acquisition was still going on at the closing date for the sections still under construction, and the report says the acquisition was held back mainly by delay in agreeing the compensation amount. Dissatisfaction persisted among the communities and households whose land was affected, and persistent local protest forced the line to be re-routed around about 3.8 km of the peri-urban edge of Jorsal in Phidim right at the end of the project; the report says there is no community resistance there now. The report adds that the Bank observed good progress in implementing the safeguard activities, that it has found the utility's safeguard performance satisfactory so far, and that the utility has committed in writing to finish the measures during construction.
cases.outcome: Only the 34.5 km first section, Damak to Godak, was physically complete when the project closed on 31 December 2016; the substations stood finished but uncommissioned for a long time because no line was there to carry power to them. An external monitor was hired to follow the resettlement plan. As of August 2018, 55 per cent of the compensation due to project-affected families had been paid. The Kathmandu Post reported in October 2019 that the Kabeli corridor had finally assumed full shape in August, after twelve years.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 203 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report counts project-affected families paid and unpaid, and gives no count of people relocated.

Table 1 of the completion report, headed Compensation payment progress and sourced in the report to 'Kabeli TL Project, August, 2018', gives 188 of 228, 41 of 82 and 673 of 1,339 with the stated reasons for each gap, and the review states the 55 per cent and repeats the three rows. cases.title: Late compensation for 2,411 people and a safety suspension on the Grand-Bassam–Aboisso–Noé road works
cases.place: Noé, Aboisso, Assouba, Samo and Port-Bouët, along the Grand-Bassam–Aboisso–Noé road, Côte d’Ivoire
cases.point: Noé, the border town opposite Elubo in Ghana, where the project built the market platform the displaced traders were moved to (village point from OpenStreetMap)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Second Phase Project of the Abidjan-Lagos Trade and Transport Facilitation Program (P116323), IDA grant H7870 of SDR 57.9 million (US$90 million equivalent) to the Republic of Côte d’Ivoire; Board approval 31 May 2012, actual closing 29 March 2019 (completion report ICR00004935, 18 December 2019; evaluation review ICRR0021995, 5 June 2020). The Bank partly suspended disbursements on Component B from December 2016 after safety and resettlement failures. The completion report rates the overall outcome Moderately Satisfactory (ICR00004935, paragraph 47); the Independent Evaluation Group also rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory (ICRR0021995).

companies.name: Projet de Facilitation du Commerce et du Transport sur le Corridor Abidjan-Lagos (PFCTCAL) Project Implementation Unit
companies.role: Implementing agency named in the completion report. It sat under the Ministry of Economy and Finance until December 2016, when it was reassigned to the Ministry of Economic Infrastructure as a condition of lifting the suspension; project management passed to the unit of the IDA-financed PRICI project on 30 November 2016. The completion report names no construction contractor.

companies.name: Ghana Highway Authority
companies.role: Road agency of Ghana’s Ministry of Roads and Highways, through its Road Safety and Environment Division; wrote the abbreviated resettlement plan for the 640 m dual carriageway and Noé bridge on the Ghanaian side, disclosed under the same project number in December 2017

cases.community: The completion report records 2,411 people affected by the works of Component B. Of those, 2,256 were compensated, which it puts at 94 per cent, and 155 could not be reached. FCFA 3.6 billion (US$7.2 million) was spent on the resettlement plan, of which FCFA 3.5 billion, 98 per cent, went directly to affected people and FCFA 56 million was placed in an escrow account. The affected people were at Port-Bouët, Samo, Assouba, Aboisso and Noé. The report says counterpart money had been set aside at appraisal so that everyone would be paid before civil works started, “however compensations were carried out with delays”, and that civil works went ahead while the resettlement plan had not been fully carried out four years into the project. At Noé the project built a platform of 8,800 square metres to move the affected traders onto; a Noé Traders Management Committee set up by Ministerial Order in June 2019 runs the new market. The borrower’s own report, printed in the completion report, says the resettlement of Noé’s traders after compensation “preserves the activities of the people affected by the project”, and that the works at the Noé parking lot were provisionally finished but had defects. On the Ghanaian side of the same crossing, the abbreviated resettlement plan of December 2017 sets a cut-off date of 19 October 2015 and counts 38 “total affected household heads/PAPs who will be losing structures and crops”, with compensation valued at GH¢389,513.95 (US$88,525.90). Payment is the responsibility of the Government of Ghana: the plan says the Ministry of Finance had already released the funds to the Ghana Highway Authority, pending the Bank’s approval of the plan. Two years after the cut-off date the plan records that “the PAPs have already stopped farming after the notification of the cut-off date”, that “continuous consultations have been going on to update the PAPs on the delay in the implementation of the RAP”, and that site visits on 27 to 29 November and 5 December 2017 found no new cocoa trees or other crops planted and nothing changed on the ground since the cut-off date, although planting around the houses had continued by agreement with the affected people until they were paid.
cases.killed_note: Five deaths are recorded on the road works and are left uncounted here because no document ties any one of them to the works. The completion report says Component B “was suspended between December 2016 and June 2017 because of serious occupational safety and road safety issues on the road works that resulted in 22 accidents, including five fatalities in 6 months” (ICR00004935, paragraph 62). The same report’s safeguards section says instead that there were “at least 22 accidents, including five fatalities, that had not been properly reported to the World Bank, and some of which had led to protests from local communities” (paragraph 71), which makes the count a floor. The report gives no cause for any individual death, does not say which of the dead were workers and which were road users, names nobody, and does not say which road section the accidents were on. Of the Component B road works, a footnote to the report records that IDA financed only the Aboisso–Noé section, about 59.2 km, the Grand-Bassam–Aboisso works being among those financed by the government’s counterpart funds, so the document does not establish which credit paid for the works where the deaths happened. The Independent Evaluation Group repeats the figure of at least 22 accidents including five fatalities, citing the report.
cases.outcome: The suspension was lifted after a nine-point action plan that moved project management to a new unit, added an environmental and a social specialist, and ordered safeguards, technical and safety audits. The road condition was improved on 113.59 km against a target of 130.3 km. The completion report says the overall safeguards were rated Moderately Unsatisfactory “during a significant period of implementation”, and that some of the accidents had led to protests from local communities.

cases.title: Twenty-three families resettled and land and crops taken for the Kribi gas plant and its pipeline road
cases.place: Mpolongwe village and the Bipaga access road, near Kribi, Océan department, South Region, Cameroon
cases.point: Mpolongwé II, the village the completion report names as the site of the power plant, 9 km north of Kribi (village point from OpenStreetMap)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Kribi Gas Power Project (P110177), IDA partial risk guarantee G-2090 of up to CFA 40 billion (US$82 million equivalent) to Kribi Power Development Company, backing the loans of local commercial lenders; Board approval 11 November 2011, effective 23 August 2012, closed in 2013 against an original closing of 2016 (completion report No. 136765-CM, 23 October 2019). The project was Environmental Category A and triggered the Bank’s policies on environmental assessment, natural habitats, physical cultural resources, indigenous peoples and involuntary resettlement. The completion report rates the overall project outcome Satisfactory (paragraph 46). No Independent Evaluation Group review of this report was reachable.

lenders.name: International Finance Corporation
lenders.role: Facility Agent for the lenders; the completion report says it led supervision of plant construction and of compliance with the Bank’s environmental and social safeguards, through an independent owner’s engineer

companies.name: Kribi Power Development Company (KPDC)
companies.role: Independent power producer created in 2008 to build and run the plant; the project’s implementing agency and borrower under the guaranteed loans

companies.name: Wartsila
companies.role: Named in the completion report as the only bidder to propose a detailed binding offer for the larger plant and as offering the lowest cost of generated electricity; the report says the choice of gas engines for the plant was made on the basis of that offer. It does not record who supplied the engines.

companies.name: Siemens France
companies.role: With KEC India, the preferred bidder for the engineering, procurement and construction contract on the 225 kV transmission line and the 11/225 kV substation

companies.name: KEC India
companies.role: Consortium partner with Siemens France on the transmission line and substation contract, as named in the completion report

companies.name: Société Nationale des Hydrocarbures (SNH)
companies.role: Cameroon’s state hydrocarbons company and sponsor of the Sanaga South gas pipeline that fuels the plant; through its Comité de Pilotage et de Suivi des Pipelines it assessed and paid the compensation for the Bipaga access road

cases.community: The completion report says the 2012 annual monitoring report recorded the physical resettlement of 23 families, compensation for crops destroyed outside the transmission line corridor, and the restoration of polluted water courses. The completion report puts the onshore gas pipeline inside the project as an associated facility, within the scope of the environmental and social impact assessment updated in 2010. For the access road from the Edéa–Kribi national road to the SNH site at Bipaga, built for SNH’s own Sanaga-Sud pipeline project, a compensation note disclosed under the Bank project in March 2012 records payments actually made: 24 people were compensated for crops in the right of way, on the basis of expert valuation sheets listing the crops, the number of plants and the amount; three private properties with land titles were partly taken, of 5,543 square metres (FCFA 27,715,000), 846 square metres (FCFA 8,460,000) and 1,360 square metres (FCFA 6,800,000); and houses lost were paid for at market economic value, with the buildings described as mostly built of temporary materials. The payments were made on 23 September 2010 and 3 December 2010, a year before the Bank’s Board approved the guarantee, out of SNH’s own budget under Prime Ministerial Decree 2010/2341/PM of 3 August 2010, some by cheque and some in cash. SNH says the payments were peaceful and on time and that no dispute was recorded, and that the people living around the access road carried on farming, fishing and working in Kribi. Once the plant was running, low-frequency noise from the engines disturbed the villages around it. Measured noise was slightly above World Health Organization and IFC levels, but so were the baseline levels taken before the plant ran, which the report puts down to the site and the nearby highways. Local communities complained of vibration in their homes. KPDC insulated the roofs of affected homes with noise-suppression material and built a noise barrier wall near the turbines. The project also had an Indigenous Peoples Plan covering Bakola communities along the transmission line; on this the completion report records only that KPDC worked with the NGO Cameroon Ecology to help carry the plan out, and gives no outcome for those communities.
cases.killed_note: The completion report records no deaths. It says no water pollution was recorded by the construction contractor and that no lost-time accidents were recorded after operations began in 2013. It gives no safety record for the construction period.
cases.displaced_label: 23 families physically resettled, from the project’s 2012 annual monitoring report as quoted in the Bank’s completion report
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 680 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report gives no other count of people relocated, and does not say where the 23 families went.
cases.outcome: The 216 MW plant was built and the completion report rates the project Satisfactory. The report also records that electricity supply from KPDC depends on the government paying a tariff compensation to the distributor ENEO to cover the gap between its costs and regulated tariffs, and that payments were irregular.

cases.title: Compensation still unpaid months after closing in Cameroon’s urban upgrading project
cases.place: Yaoundé, with works also in Douala, Bamenda, Maroua and Mbalmayo, Cameroon
cases.point: Yaoundé, the city where the completion report says two compensation payments were still waiting for presidential clearance (city point from OpenStreetMap); the project’s Phase 2 resettlement plans cover the Kondengui and Ekounou quarters of Yaoundé 4 and the Efoulan and Nsimeyong quarters

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Urban and Water Development Support Project, known as PDUE (P084002), IDA credit 4313-CM of SDR 53.3 million (US$80 million equivalent) and an additional financing, credit 4820-CM, of SDR 18.9 million (US$28.7 million equivalent) from Pilot Crisis Response Window resources; Board approval 29 May 2007, actual closing 31 August 2015 (completion report ICR00003619, 29 February 2016; evaluation review ICRR0020199, 28 June 2016). Category B, triggering the Bank’s policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. Both documents rate the overall outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the risk to development outcome High.

companies.name: Project Coordination Unit, Ministry of Housing and Urban Development (MINHDU)
companies.role: Implementing agency for the urban components, a unit kept inside MINHDU after closing; it paid compensation directly or through the municipalities. The completion report names no construction contractor.

cases.community: The completion report says counterpart money was secured so that the project unit, directly or through the municipalities, could pay compensation to the 585 people affected by the project. Of those, 88 per cent had been compensated as of 31 January 2016, against 51 per cent at the closing date of 31 August 2015, for CFAF 401 million, which the report puts at 88 per cent of the amount due. The report says payments had markedly progressed since the closing date “but two for Yaoundé were still awaiting the presidential clearance at the time of this report”. The Bank’s involuntary resettlement policy was rated only partly complied with, Moderately Unsatisfactory in early 2014 and again at closing. The report says the delays were beyond the project’s control: the national rules for taking land and paying for it ran through several administrative steps, including a Presidential Decree clearing the list of affected people that could take months to come out, and further decrees were needed to add people left out of the first assessments. Phase 2 resettlement plans were approved only at the end of 2014. For Phase 1 the report says no standalone resettlement plans had been prepared where works cut across parts of urban plots, while adding that “in practice though, as noted in supervision reports, the PCU had complied with the policy’s requirements through consultations on the project’ benefits”. It says that in many cases owners agreed to hand land over to the public domain with no money paid, which saved time on the works, and that other families were paid for damage. For Phase 2 the rule was tightened so that works could not start before people were paid. The report says full payment of the outstanding compensation “remains of utmost importance”, and that the Bank made fully resolving the compensation legacy a condition of approving a follow-on operation.
cases.killed_note: Neither the completion report nor the Independent Evaluation Group’s review records a death or an injury on this project.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 536 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report counts 585 people affected and gives no count of anyone relocated.
cases.outcome: Payments had moved on since the closing date but were not finished when the completion report was written in February 2016, with two for Yaoundé awaiting presidential clearance. The Bank attached the condition that the compensation legacy be fully resolved before the follow-on “Inclusive Cities” operation went to its Board.

cases.point: Riviéra 2, Cocody, Abidjan, the site of the underpass where the ten shop employees worked (neighbourhood point from OpenStreetMap)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Emergency Urban Infrastructure Project (P110020), IDA grant H397-CI of SDR 57.10 million (US$94 million equivalent) and an additional grant H591-CI of SDR 33.10 million (US$50 million equivalent), of which SDR 9.93 million (US$15 million equivalent) came from Pilot Crisis Response Window resources; Board approval 12 June 2008, closing 31 March 2014 against an original date of 15 September 2012 (completion report ICR00003208, 29 January 2015; evaluation review ICRR14735, 20 April 2015). Category B, triggering the Bank’s policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. cases.community: Resettlement plans were prepared for four sites in Abidjan: the footbridge at Williamsville, the underpass at Riviera 2, the road at M’Badon, and the bridge and connecting road over the ravine in Cocody. The borrower’s report, printed as an annex to the completion report, says unforeseen impacts on local residents occurred during the rehabilitation of the M’Badon road, where access to shops was restricted, and during the construction of the Cocody zone 7-9 bridge, where third parties were damaged when a site access road was opened. For those cases it says the coordination unit “has ensured that Project-Affected Persons (PAPs) were duly compensated”, and that “a total of 629 PAPs have been compensated to the amount of FCFA 857,568,478 for a total of 639 PAPs identified. It remains to reimburse the salaries of 10 store employees affected by the Riviera 2 constructions due to technical unemployment, for whom salaries were pre-financed by employers, who have however failed to produce documentary evidence of this pre-financing to justify their refund.” On the annex’s account the ten were paid their wages by their employers; what remained unpaid was the project’s reimbursement of those wages. The same annex says an environmental and social review mission recruited in 2012 confirmed compliance with the project’s safeguard instruments. The main text of the same completion report says instead that the plans “provided compensation to all 639 persons affected by temporary closures causing loss of income due to works at these sites”, and that no other safeguard action was needed and the safeguards rating was satisfactory throughout.
cases.killed_note: Neither the completion report nor the Independent Evaluation Group’s review records a death or an injury on this project.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 519 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The documents count 639 people affected by temporary closures and loss of income, and no one relocated.
cases.outcome: The reimbursement of the ten store employees’ wages was still outstanding when the completion report was written in January 2015, the annex giving as the reason that the employers who had pre-financed those wages had not produced documentary evidence of it. The Independent Evaluation Group’s review repeats the completion report’s main text that all 639 affected people were compensated and does not mention the ten.
