cases.community: The water component extended the distribution network into poor quarters in the south and south-west of Kinshasa, in the communes of Mont Ngafula, Ngaliema, Lemba and Selembao, and built two reservoirs on the Mont Kimwenza Sebo and Kimbondo hills, a pumping station, and a catchment plant on the Lukaya river. Every count of the people is the June 2010 resettlement plan’s, written before the works began. It counts 72 households affected and 245 people in them: 41 at the first reservoir site, 7 at the pumping station, 5 at the second reservoir and 19 at the Lukaya site. Of the 72, it counts 30 losing land or structures, 23 losing their housing and 19 losing crops. It records the destruction across the three hill sites of various buildings, small houses, fences and foundations, and at the Lukaya site 72 fruit trees and 3 food gardens of cassava, and a permanent loss of 9,306 square metres of cultivable land, which it gives as 517 market-garden beds. The completion report says the start of works was put off from November 2009, when the contract was awarded, to January 2011, over who should pay the compensation and clear the sites. Cash indemnities of US$1,215,322 were then paid to the people affected by the water component. A non-governmental organisation was hired to help them put the money into income-generating work; 72 heads of household were trained in how to use their compensation that way, which the report says benefited 245 people in the affected households. The completion report concludes that all works were carried out in full respect of the safeguards instruments and that the Bank’s environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement policies were fully complied with, while noting that the frameworks themselves were prepared 13 months after the project became effective, against the six months the financing agreement allowed, and that the Bank’s team and management “ensured that no construction works took place prior to the completion and disclosure of the safeguards instruments”.
cases.killed_note: Neither the completion report nor the Independent Evaluation Group’s review records a death or an injury on this project.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 245 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The 72 households, the 245 people and the breakdown of 30 losing land or structures, 23 losing their housing and 19 losing crops are all figures from the June 2010 resettlement plan, written before the works started in January 2011, not counts from an outcome document. The completion report carries the same two figures but attaches them to something else: it says 72 heads of household were trained in how to use their compensation for income-generating activities, “benefiting 245 people in the affected households”. No document reachable here says how many people were actually moved or where they went.
cases.outcome: The compensation was paid and the works went ahead from January 2011. The completion report records no unpaid balance and no dispute over the payments.

cases.community: The completion report says the government had to spend money it had set aside for its own share of the project on “unforeseen social measures that needed to be taken during the resettlement of communities living near the Takon landfill”. Those measures were three classroom blocks, eight toilets, roads, clinics, a community centre, electricity and a small-scale water supply, amounting to CFA 830 million, and the report says they were supplied to compensate communities whose land was taken to build the landfill at Takon, near Porto-Novo. Because that money went on the compensation, the government could not meet its 10 per cent share of the original credit or its 15 per cent share of the additional financing, and in July 2011 asked for funds to be reallocated. The Independent Evaluation Group’s review gives the same account and adds that the landfill was not operating when the project closed: delays at the National Board for Procurement Control meant the operator’s contract was not signed until six months after the closing date. A footnote in the completion report records that resettlement was not planned during the programme’s first phase, but “some resettlement activity took place without a resettlement framework being in place”. Both documents say the project complied with all safeguard requirements, that resettlement action plans were prepared and carried out before civil works began, and that the Benin Environment Agency certified the works; the completion report rates safeguards satisfactory.
cases.killed_note: Neither the completion report nor the Independent Evaluation Group’s review records a death or an injury on this project.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 243 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. Neither Bank document counts the households or people whose land was taken at Takon, or anyone relocated.
cases.outcome: The communities received the buildings and services rather than cash. The landfill they gave up land for was still not being exploited at project closure, the operator’s contract being signed six months after the closing date; the Independent Evaluation Group’s review says the landfill was “still not fully functional by project closure”.

companies.role: Named in the project’s February 2019 mission report as the contractor on the Avenue Gazumbu works in Kolwezi, where the mission was also to check that the firm’s environmental officer and sociologist had been put on site and to visit its camp and borrow pits

cases.community: The completion report counts 1,078 people affected by the project, identified through resettlement plans, of whom 1,041 were compensated for a total of US$155,918. The report says the rest did not present themselves to receive compensation, that the secretariat and local authorities tried to locate and contact them in each case, and that US$18,984 has been reserved with the local governments should those efforts succeed; it does not print a figure for how many people that is. Seventy-nine occupational health and safety incidents were recorded. Seventy-five were minor, three were serious and one, a fall from height causing serious injury, was treated as severe and reported to Bank management through its incident response procedure; the report says root causes were analysed, corrective measures developed, and the secretariat supplied documentation of the injured person’s treatment and full recovery. Three cases of non-compliance were documented. Two were works starting before the resettlement plan had been carried out, one of them before the contract had even been signed; in one of those the Bank told the government the investment would not be eligible for project money and no project funds were used, which a footnote gives as the reason no infrastructure was financed by the project in Goma, and in the other the resettlement plan was updated and the works allowed to continue. In Kolwezi, a project mission in February 2019 found 13 people losing income on Avenue Gazumbu — among them a hairdresser, a phone-kiosk operator and a pharmacy seller, listed by name, with GPS points, and assessed at US$1,195 in all, of which US$150 was assistance to people counted as vulnerable — whom an earlier consultant had missed: the 2016 study reported finding no affected people on that avenue, so no resettlement plan was written, no cut-off date was published and no signs were put up to stop new occupation of the right of way. The mayor’s office said it was ready to pay the 13 so they would clear the route before works began. At Kananga, the project’s own report on carrying out the resettlement plan for the erosion-control works at the MONUSCO site records that on 16 June 2021 one household head, counted as 15 affected persons, was paid US$5,650, all of what the plan provided: US$4,000 for the house and US$1,600 for fruit trees and family crops, with US$50 for one person assessed as vulnerable. Kananga city hall put up US$4,000 of that and the project US$1,650, in a table the report heads as funds for paying affected people who had been left out. The report says the household, that of Laurent Nkashama, moved into a house bought on the spot before the old one was pulled down, that the operation passed without incident, and that a grievance committee opened its registers at the town hall and in Mulombodi quarter on 19 June 2021.
cases.suppression: The completion report records that a person who had told the Bank of a possible failure of compliance on a construction site in Mbandaka “was allegedly subsequently threatened by provincial authorities”. The Bank sent a field mission at once, which it says confirmed both that the site complied and that the complainant was safe; a safeguards compliance audit followed and found no other case of non-compliance, and the Bank says it kept in regular touch with the complainant. The Independent Evaluation Group’s review records the same episode, without the word allegedly, as “a complainant reported being threatened by the provincial authorities after reporting a potential lack of compliance on a construction site in Mbandaka”. The review also divides the three cases of non-compliance differently from the completion report, counting works started before the contract was signed and works started before the resettlement plan was carried out as two separate cases.
cases.killed_note: Neither document records a death. The severe safety incident was a fall from height; the completion report says the injured person was treated and fully recovered.
cases.displaced_label: 15 people in one household resettled from Avenue Lithanie, Mulombodi quarter, Kananga, in the project’s own June 2021 report on carrying out the resettlement plan
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 230 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The 15 is the only count of people actually resettled in any outcome document reachable here; the completion report’s 1,078 is a count of people affected across all the project cities.
cases.outcome: All the safety cases and the grievances were recorded as closed before the project ended. US$18,984 of compensation stayed unpaid, reserved with local governments for the affected people who never came forward. The completion report rates the project Moderately Unsatisfactory overall, and says Kananga still faces serious gully erosion threatening other infrastructure.

fields_add.community: On the Ethiopian side the completion report records a fatal accident: a local employee died when a company vehicle he was driving was swept away during heavy floods. Ethiopian Electric Power gave the financiers a detailed report on the death, with an assessment of safeguards and health and safety compliance, which the completion report says the financiers deemed satisfactory. On the Kenyan side the same report records a fatal accident in February 2017 involving a contractor's employee under Lot 4, without giving a cause; the utility shared the full report with the financiers and the Bank judged health and safety compliance satisfactory. The livestock feed processing plant built for those who lost the grazing land was completed only after protracted delays, with the affected people then organising themselves into a cooperative to run it. As part of livelihood restoration in Ethiopia, 25 settlements holding more than 3,000 households were given mini-grid electricity under the project. Theft of materials from the transmission towers led to heavier surveillance and a redesign of the towers with a barrier to make them harder to climb.
